Foods served on a stick.Corn dog: Hot dogs dipped in cornmeal batter and deep-fried are a US state-fair staple, and the stick was designed to make them a one-handed snack.
Foods served on a stick.Shish kebab: The name comes from Turkish for skewer roasted meat. Tradition says soldiers once grilled meat on their swords over open fires.
Foods served on a stick.Lollipop: Hard candy on a stick was a simple idea, but the handle changed it: a sweet you could suck for ages without sticky fingers.
Foods served on a stick.Popsicle: An 11-year-old, Frank Epperson, reportedly left soda and a stirring stick outside on a freezing night in 1905 and invented it by accident.
Foods served on a stick.Satay: Skewered, grilled marinated meat served with peanut sauce is a favorite across Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, often cooked over charcoal on street carts.
Foods served on a stick.Yakitori: Japanese for grilled bird, it covers skewered chicken, and the menu goes beyond thigh: hearts, skin and cartilage are all popular cuts.
Foods served on a stick.Candy apple: A whole apple dipped in hard red sugar syrup, supposedly invented in 1908 by a New Jersey candymaker experimenting with red cinnamon candy.
Foods served on a stick.Cake pop: Crumbled cake mixed with frosting, rolled into balls and dipped in chocolate; the treat was popularized in the late 2000s by the blogger Bakerella.
Foods served on a stick.Souvlaki: Greek for little skewer, it is grilled meat on a stick, usually pork, and Greeks often eat it straight off the skewer or in pita.
Foods served on a stick.Cotton candy: Spun sugar on a paper cone is mostly air; an early machine version debuted at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair and sold over 68,000 boxes.
Foods served on a stick.Dango: Chewy Japanese rice-flour dumplings, usually three or four on one skewer, and in spring they appear pink, white and green for flower viewing.
Foods served on a stick.Tanghulu: This traditional Chinese street snack is fruit, often hawthorn berries, coated in a glassy sugar shell that cracks when you bite it.
Foods served on a stick.Magnum: The ice cream bar on a stick, first sold in 1989 in Sweden, has a thick chocolate shell that you break with the first bite.
Foods served on a stick.Hot dog: A trap: despite being the classic ballpark food, it sits in a bun and is not served on a stick; only the corn dog gets one.
Foods served on a stick.Taco: A trap: a folded tortilla filled with ingredients has no stick, and its shell is the only holder it needs; Mexican tacos date back centuries.
Foods served on a stick.Burrito: The name means little donkey in Spanish, probably because the rolled tortilla resembled a pack load; it needs no stick, just foil.
Foods served on a stick.Pizza: It is eaten from a slice or a plate, not a stick; Naples' traditional version is baked in a 450-degree-Celsius oven in about a minute.
Foods served on a stick.Soup: Soup is a liquid, so a stick is useless; the oldest known evidence of soup-making is around 20,000 years ago, once pottery could hold hot water.
Foods served on a stick.Sushi: Sushi is usually eaten with fingers or chopsticks, not on a stick; the original dish was fermented fish packed in rice to preserve it.
Foods served on a stick.Ice cream sandwich: It is ice cream between two cookies or wafers and held by hand, no stick; it became a New York street staple in the early 1900s.
Foods served on a stick.Pancake: Pancakes are stacked flat on a plate, not skewered, but pancakes on a stick do exist as a novelty; they are among the oldest cooked foods.
Foods served on a stick.Spring roll: Spring rolls are eaten by hand or with chopsticks, not on a stick; the name comes from the Chinese tradition of eating them at spring festival.
Foods served on a stick.Cupcake: Cupcakes sit in a paper liner and are eaten by hand; the name may come from the cup used to measure ingredients, or from baking in cups.
Foods served on a stick.Nachos: Nachos were invented in 1943 at a restaurant in Piedras Negras, Mexico, by Ignacio Anaya, and they are served as a pile of chips, no stick.

Landlocked countries outside Europe.Bolivia: Bolivia lost its Pacific coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879-84), and still keeps a navy for Lake Titicaca and its rivers.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Paraguay: One of two landlocked countries in South America. Its trade flows down the Paraguay and Paraná rivers to the Atlantic.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Nepal: Home to Everest and seven other of the world's ten tallest peaks. Nepal's flag is the only national flag that is not rectangular.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Bhutan: This Himalayan kingdom measures national progress by Gross National Happiness, and is carbon negative thanks to its forests.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Mongolia: One of the least densely populated countries on Earth, and it's the largest landlocked country in the world by area.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Laos: Landlocked Laos is the only such country in Southeast Asia, and the Mekong River runs along much of its western border.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Afghanistan: Surrounded by Pakistan, Iran and Central Asia, it has been a crossroads of the Silk Road for thousands of years.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Chad: Landlocked in north-central Africa, Chad holds much of Lake Chad, which has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Mali: Landlocked in West Africa, Mali was home to Timbuktu, a medieval center of learning with famed manuscript libraries.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Niger: A West African country named for the Niger River. It is landlocked, and mostly covered by the Sahara.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Ethiopia: It lost its coast when Eritrea became independent in 1993. Ethiopia is Africa's second most populous nation and the home of coffee.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Uganda: Landlocked, but it holds much of Lake Victoria, Africa's largest lake. The Nile begins its journey north there.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Rwanda: Known as the 'land of a thousand hills'. It's landlocked, and a rare home for mountain gorillas.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Kazakhstan: The world's biggest landlocked country by area is ninth largest overall. It borders the Caspian Sea, which is a lake and not an ocean.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Peru: Peru has a long Pacific coastline, so it is not landlocked. Machu Picchu is its signature site.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Chile: A narrow country running over 4,000 kilometers down South America's Pacific edge, so it has a great deal of coast.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Bangladesh: It has a coast on the Bay of Bengal. It also holds the world's largest delta shared with India.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Myanmar: It has a long coastline on the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal, which makes it a trap among its Asian neighbors.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Cameroon: Cameroon has a coast on the Gulf of Guinea. Its geography, from coast to mountains, earns it the nickname 'Africa in miniature'.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Kenya: Kenya has a coast on the Indian Ocean, with the historic port of Mombasa, which makes it not landlocked.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Somalia: It has Africa's longest mainland coastline, running along the Indian Ocean and the Gulf of Aden.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Iran: Iran borders both the Caspian Sea to the north and the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman to the south, so it isn't landlocked.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Ecuador: Named for the equator, which crosses it. It has a Pacific coast and also owns the Galápagos Islands.
Landlocked countries outside Europe.Vietnam: A long S-shaped country with over 3,000 kilometers of coast on the South China Sea.

Korean dishes.Bibimbap: The name means 'mixed rice'; it is served with vegetables, meat and a fried egg, and a stone pot version gives the rice a crisp bottom.
Korean dishes.Bulgogi: The name means 'fire meat'; thin slices of beef are marinated in soy, sugar and pear juice, whose enzymes help tenderize it.
Korean dishes.Kimchi: Fermented vegetables, most famously napa cabbage, eaten with almost every Korean meal; thousands of varieties exist.
Korean dishes.Japchae: Chewy glass noodles made from sweet potato starch, stir-fried with vegetables, traditionally served at festive occasions and banquets.
Korean dishes.Tteokbokki: Chewy rice cakes simmered in a fiery red gochujang sauce, a hugely popular street food that was once made with soy sauce.
Korean dishes.Kimbap: Rolled rice and fillings wrapped in seaweed that looks like sushi but is seasoned with sesame oil, not vinegar.
Korean dishes.Samgyeopsal: Thick slices of pork belly grilled at the table, then wrapped in lettuce leaves with garlic and ssamjang sauce.
Korean dishes.Galbi: Marinated beef or pork short ribs, grilled at the table, and a classic dish for celebrations and family meals.
Korean dishes.Bingsu: A mountain of shaved ice topped with sweet red beans and fruit, and the Korean cousin of other shaved ice desserts, popular in summer.
Korean dishes.Hotteok: A sweet pancake filled with brown sugar and nuts, a winter street snack that came from Chinese traders in the 1800s.
Korean dishes.Pajeon: Scallion pancake, traditionally served with makgeolli (rice wine) on rainy days, which Koreans say sounds like sizzling rain.
Korean dishes.Sushi: Sushi is Japanese; the similar-looking Korean dish kimbap is seasoned with sesame oil rather than vinegar.
Korean dishes.Gyoza: Pan-fried dumplings borrowed by Japan from Chinese jiaozi after the Second World War, so they aren't Korean (their Korean cousin is mandu).
Korean dishes.Pho: Vietnam's national noodle soup with a fragrant beef broth, not Korean.
Korean dishes.Pad thai: A Thai dish of stir-fried rice noodles, nothing to do with Korean cuisine.
Korean dishes.Dim sum: Dim sum is Cantonese, and its small steamed bites are a tradition from Chinese teahouses.
Korean dishes.Tempura: Japanese, not Korean: the batter-frying technique is thought to have come from Portuguese traders in the 1500s.
Korean dishes.Laksa: A Malaysian and Singaporean noodle soup with a spicy coconut or sour broth, so it isn't Korean.
Korean dishes.Rendang: A slow-cooked dry curry from the Minangkabau of Indonesia, once voted among the world's best foods in a CNN poll.
Korean dishes.Teriyaki: A Japanese cooking style: 'teri' means glaze and 'yaki' means grilled, so the dish is Japanese, not Korean.
Korean dishes.Mapo tofu: A Sichuan classic of soft tofu in a numbing, spicy sauce, named for the pockmarked old woman who supposedly invented it.
Korean dishes.Takoyaki: Japanese octopus balls from Osaka, not Korean; the batter is poured into special moulds and flipped with skewers.
Korean dishes.Peking duck: A Chinese classic that dates back centuries and is famously served in three courses in some restaurants.
Korean dishes.Tom yum: Thailand's hot and sour soup with lemongrass and galangal, not Korean, even though Korean soups can be fiery too.

Edible mushrooms.Shiitake: Japanese for 'oak mushroom', it's traditionally grown on oak logs, and the second most-cultivated edible mushroom.
Edible mushrooms.Portobello: Portobello is just a fully grown cremini, which is the same species as the white button mushroom.
Edible mushrooms.Chanterelle: The golden trumpet smells faintly of apricots and defies cultivation, so every one is foraged.
Edible mushrooms.Porcini: The Italian name means 'little pigs', and the king bolete is prized dried and fresh.
Edible mushrooms.Morel: Its honeycomb cap must be cooked, as raw ones cause stomach upset, and false morels can be toxic.
Edible mushrooms.Oyster mushroom: It paralyzes nematodes with toxins to feed on them, so this mushroom is a small carnivore.
Edible mushrooms.Enoki: The long white ones in shops are grown in the dark, while the wild form is short and brown.
Edible mushrooms.Button mushroom: The white button is the youngest, the same species as cremini and portobello, picked at different ages.
Edible mushrooms.Cremini: Also known as baby bella, the brown form is the same species as the white button and the portobello.
Edible mushrooms.Maitake: Its Japanese name means 'dancing mushroom', and it is called hen-of-the-woods in English.
Edible mushrooms.King trumpet: Also called king oyster, its thick stem is sliced into discs that sear like scallops.
Edible mushrooms.Lion's mane: Its shaggy white look gives it its name, and cooks say its texture resembles crab or lobster.
Edible mushrooms.Death cap: It causes most deadly mushroom poisonings worldwide, because it looks like edible ones.
Edible mushrooms.Fly agaric: The red cap with white spots is classic fairy-tale imagery, but it is toxic and psychoactive.
Edible mushrooms.Destroying angel: A pure white deadly Amanita; a bite of it can cause liver failure.
Edible mushrooms.Nori: This is dried seaweed, an alga, not a mushroom. It wraps sushi rolls.
Edible mushrooms.Kelp: A large brown seaweed, so an alga rather than a fungus, and it grows into underwater forests.
Edible mushrooms.Spirulina: A blue-green cyanobacterium, once harvested by Aztecs, not a mushroom.
Edible mushrooms.Tempeh: Fermented soybeans bound by Rhizopus mold, a fungus but not a mushroom, from Indonesia.
Edible mushrooms.Yeast: A single-celled fungus that makes bread rise, not a mushroom, yet a relative.
Edible mushrooms.Artichoke: The edible part is an unopened flower bud of a thistle, not a fungus.
Edible mushrooms.Eggplant: It's a nightshade fruit, so a botanical berry, and not a mushroom, despite meaty texture.
Edible mushrooms.Shallot: A small onion relative with a milder bite, and a plant, not a fungus.
Edible mushrooms.Water chestnut: It's neither water nor nut, but a crunchy aquatic corm, so a plant, not a mushroom.

Apple varieties.Granny Smith: Maria Ann Smith found the seedling in Australia in the 1860s, and its green sour taste suits baking.
Apple varieties.Fuji: It was bred in Japan in the 1930s and released in 1962, and today is the world's most-grown apple.
Apple varieties.Gala: It came from New Zealand in the 1930s, bred from Kidd's Orange Red and Golden Delicious.
Apple varieties.Honeycrisp: Developed at the University of Minnesota and released in 1991, its big cells make it explosively crisp.
Apple varieties.Golden Delicious: A chance seedling in West Virginia around 1900, and it's the parent of many newer varieties.
Apple varieties.Pink Lady: Pink Lady is a trademark name for the Cripps Pink variety from Australia.
Apple varieties.Braeburn: A chance seedling in New Zealand in the 1950s, with a crisp texture and complex taste.
Apple varieties.Red Delicious: Discovered in Iowa in the 1870s as 'Hawkeye', its name came from marketing, and it was once America's most-grown apple.
Apple varieties.McIntosh: Canadian John McIntosh found it in 1811, and Apple's Macintosh computer was named for it.
Apple varieties.Jazz: A New Zealand variety from the 1980s, crossing Braeburn and Royal Gala, and it's crisp and sweet.
Apple varieties.Cox: Cox's Orange Pippin was raised in England in the 1820s by a retired brewer named Richard Cox.
Apple varieties.Jonagold: Raised in New York in 1943 from Jonathan and Golden Delicious, a large, sweet-tart apple.
Apple varieties.Bramley: The classic British cooking apple grew from a seed planted by Mary Ann Brailsford around 1809 in Nottinghamshire.
Apple varieties.Bartlett: It's a pear, not an apple. Bartlett is the main canning pear in the US and is called Williams in Europe.
Apple varieties.Bosc: A pear, with a long neck and russet skin, which stays firm when baked.
Apple varieties.Anjou: A pear whose skin turns from green to yellow, and it's good for eating fresh.
Apple varieties.Comice: A winter pear, so juicy and creamy, and called the queen of pears.
Apple varieties.Conference: The most common pear in Britain, long and green with a firm texture, so not an apple.
Apple varieties.Yukon Gold: A potato, not an apple, with golden flesh, and was bred in Canada in the 1960s.
Apple varieties.Maris Piper: A potato that is the British favorite for roasting and chips, not an apple.
Apple varieties.King Edward: A potato from Britain, created in 1902, with a fluffy interior, not an apple.
Apple varieties.Concord: A grape, with a deep purple and a taste of grape juice and jam, not an apple.
Apple varieties.Clementine: It's a citrus fruit, a seedless mandarin type, not an apple.
Apple varieties.Medjool: A large, caramel-sweet date, known as the king of dates, and not an apple.

Former Soviet republics.Ukraine: Europe's largest country entirely within the continent, famed for black-soil farmland that earned it the nickname breadbasket of Europe.
Former Soviet republics.Belarus: Its Białowieża Forest, shared with Poland, shelters Europe's largest wild bison herd and is one of the last primeval lowland forests.
Former Soviet republics.Kazakhstan: The world's largest landlocked country, it hosts the Baikonur Cosmodrome, where Yuri Gagarin launched in 1961.
Former Soviet republics.Georgia: This Caucasus country claims one of the world's oldest winemaking traditions, with 8,000-year-old evidence of wine in clay vessels.
Former Soviet republics.Armenia: In 301 AD it became the first nation to adopt Christianity as its state religion, long before Rome did.
Former Soviet republics.Azerbaijan: Nicknamed the Land of Fire for natural gas flames, its capital Baku sits on the Caspian Sea and its oil fields were among the first drilled.
Former Soviet republics.Estonia: A tiny Baltic nation that gave the world Skype and runs nearly all government services online, even letting people vote by internet.
Former Soviet republics.Latvia: Over half of this Baltic country is forest, and its capital Riga has Europe's largest collection of Art Nouveau buildings.
Former Soviet republics.Lithuania: It was the last pagan state in Europe, converting to Christianity only in 1387, and in 1990 was the first republic to declare independence from the USSR.
Former Soviet republics.Moldova: Its Milestii Mici cellar holds a wine collection of millions of bottles, one of the largest in the world, in underground limestone tunnels.
Former Soviet republics.Uzbekistan: Samarkand and Bukhara, jewels of the Silk Road, are here, and it is one of only two doubly landlocked countries.
Former Soviet republics.Kyrgyzstan: Mountains cover most of this Central Asian country, and its nomadic heritage lives on in yurts and the epic poem Manas.
Former Soviet republics.Tajikistan: Over 90 percent of it is mountainous, and the Pamir range here is nicknamed the Roof of the World.
Former Soviet republics.Poland: It was a Soviet satellite in the Warsaw Pact, yet never one of the 15 republics, and its Solidarity movement helped topple communism.
Former Soviet republics.Hungary: A satellite state of the USSR, not a republic; its 1956 uprising was crushed by Soviet tanks.
Former Soviet republics.Czech Republic: Part of Czechoslovakia, a Warsaw Pact state under Soviet influence but never a Soviet republic, it split peacefully from Slovakia in 1993.
Former Soviet republics.Romania: It was in the Soviet sphere but kept some independence; its 1989 revolution was the only violent overthrow in the Eastern Bloc.
Former Soviet republics.Bulgaria: A close Soviet ally, so loyal it was sometimes called the 16th republic, though it was formally independent.
Former Soviet republics.Mongolia: The Soviet Union's closest satellite, yet technically independent, and the world's least densely populated sovereign country.
Former Soviet republics.Finland: A trap: Finland was part of the Russian Empire, but the Soviets never annexed it after the 1939 Winter War, where it held them off.
Former Soviet republics.Afghanistan: The Soviets invaded in 1979 and fought a decade-long war, but it never became a Soviet republic.
Former Soviet republics.Albania: Communist, but it broke with Moscow in 1961 and aligned with China, so it was never a republic of the USSR.
Former Soviet republics.Slovakia: Part of Czechoslovakia in the Soviet bloc, it has been independent since 1993 and was never a Soviet republic.
Former Soviet republics.Serbia: Once part of Yugoslavia, a communist state that broke with Stalin in 1948 and was never under the Soviet umbrella as a republic.

Mountain ranges in Europe.Alps: Europe's best-known range stretches across eight countries, and Mont Blanc at 4,806 meters is its highest peak.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Pyrenees: The range between France and Spain shelters tiny Andorra, and its highest peak, Aneto, tops 3,400 meters.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Carpathians: This arc runs about 1,500 km through Central and Eastern Europe, and holds Europe's biggest populations of brown bears outside Russia.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Apennines: The spine of Italy runs the length of the peninsula, and its Gran Sasso hosts the southernmost glacier in Europe.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Dolomites: Italian peaks of pale rock that glow pink at sunset, a phenomenon locals call enrosadira, and a UNESCO site.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Dinaric Alps: A rugged range along the Adriatic through Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia, and the origin of the word karst for limestone landscapes.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Balkan Mountains: The range crossing Bulgaria gave its name to the whole Balkan Peninsula, and the Shipka Pass has a famous battle.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Jura: A limestone range between France and Switzerland, whose name was given to the Jurassic period.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Vosges: A forested range in eastern France along the Rhine, with its rounded peaks known as ballons.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Black Forest: A wooded highland in southwest Germany, known for cuckoo clocks and the Danube's source, and a cake is named after it.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Tatras: The highest part of the Carpathians, on the Polish and Slovak border, with peaks up to about 2,650 meters.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Picos de Europa: A range in northern Spain, so named because sailors returning from the Americas saw its peaks first.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Cairngorms: Scotland's high range has the largest national park in Britain, and a population of reindeer introduced in 1952.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Atlas: The range stretches across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, and it is in Africa.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Andes: The longest continental mountain range in the world, running about 7,000 km down the west of South America.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Rockies: North America's range runs from Canada to New Mexico, and it is on another continent.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Himalayas: The Asian range with Everest, whose name means abode of snow in Sanskrit.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Appalachians: An old range in eastern North America, much older and lower than the Alps.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Drakensberg: South Africa's highest range, whose name is Afrikaans for dragon mountains.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Zagros: A long range in Iran and Iraq, which is in Asia.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Altai: A range where Russia, China, Mongolia and Kazakhstan meet, in Asia.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Hindu Kush: A range in Afghanistan and Pakistan, in Asia, with peaks over 7,000 meters.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Cascades: A volcanic range in the northwestern United States, including Mount St. Helens.
Mountain ranges in Europe.Sierra Madre: Mexico's chain of ranges runs along both coasts, in North America.

Animals native to the Arctic.Polar bear: Its skin is black and its fur is transparent, not white. The largest land carnivore, it hunts seals from sea ice.
Animals native to the Arctic.Walrus: Both sexes have tusks, which can be a meter long. They help haul the walrus up on ice, and they gather in herds of thousands.
Animals native to the Arctic.Arctic fox: Its coat turns from brown in summer to white in winter. It can survive temperatures well below minus 40 degrees Celsius.
Animals native to the Arctic.Narwhal: The 'unicorn of the sea' has a tusk that is a very long tooth, up to 3 meters, and it is full of nerve endings.
Animals native to the Arctic.Beluga: Called 'canaries of the sea' for their chirps and whistles. They are white as adults and live in Arctic and subarctic waters.
Animals native to the Arctic.Snowy owl: A white owl that hunts by day in summer, since the Arctic sun never sets. Harry Potter's Hedwig was one.
Animals native to the Arctic.Musk ox: A shaggy survivor from the Ice Age. Adults form a circle with calves in the middle when wolves threaten, and its underwool, qiviut, is prized.
Animals native to the Arctic.Reindeer: Called caribou in North America. Both sexes grow antlers, and their eyes change color between summer and winter.
Animals native to the Arctic.Arctic hare: A big white hare that can hop on its hind legs like a kangaroo. It lives in the far north, and huddles in groups of hundreds.
Animals native to the Arctic.Lemming: A small rodent. The myth of mass suicide jumping off cliffs came from a staged scene in a 1958 Disney film.
Animals native to the Arctic.Bowhead whale: May be the longest-lived mammal, with some individuals over 200 years old. Its massive skull can break through ice.
Animals native to the Arctic.Ringed seal: The main food of polar bears. It keeps breathing holes open in the ice and builds snow dens to raise pups.
Animals native to the Arctic.Emperor penguin: A trap: the largest penguin lives in Antarctica, at the opposite end of the Earth. There are no penguins at the North Pole.
Animals native to the Arctic.Adelie penguin: Lives on Antarctica's coast, not in the Arctic. It's named for the wife of French explorer Dumont d'Urville.
Animals native to the Arctic.Leopard seal: A fearsome Antarctic predator that hunts penguins. It lives around the South Pole, not the Arctic.
Animals native to the Arctic.Weddell seal: Lives farther south than any other mammal, in Antarctica. It can dive for over an hour under the ice.
Animals native to the Arctic.Wandering albatross: A southern ocean bird with the longest wingspan of any living bird, up to 3.5 meters. It's found far from the Arctic.
Animals native to the Arctic.Kangaroo: Native to Australia and New Guinea. Its hot climate is about as far from the Arctic as one gets.
Animals native to the Arctic.Camel: A desert animal, though Bactrian camels cope with cold winters in Asia. It's not native to the Arctic.
Animals native to the Arctic.Lion: An African big cat, not from the Arctic. Lions live in groups, called prides, unlike most cats.
Animals native to the Arctic.Toucan: A tropical bird of Central and South America, with a big beak that helps it shed heat. It's far from any ice.
Animals native to the Arctic.Iguana: A reptile that needs warmth since it can't generate its own body heat. It could not survive the Arctic cold.
Animals native to the Arctic.Gorilla: A great ape native to the forests of central Africa. The Arctic is much too cold for it.
Animals native to the Arctic.Macaw: A colorful parrot of Central and South American rainforests. It can live over 50 years in captivity.

Animals with more than four legs.Spider: Spiders have eight legs, which helps tell them apart from insects. Their legs move partly by hydraulic pressure, not only muscles.
Animals with more than four legs.Ant: Ants have six legs, like all insects. They can carry many times their own weight, and some species form living bridges with their bodies.
Animals with more than four legs.Crab: Crabs have ten legs, though the front pair are pincers. They walk sideways because their joints bend that way.
Animals with more than four legs.Centipede: Centipedes have one pair of legs per segment, and the count is always an odd number of pairs. None has exactly 100 legs, despite the name.
Animals with more than four legs.Scorpion: Scorpions have eight legs plus a pair of pincers. Under ultraviolet light they glow blue-green.
Animals with more than four legs.Lobster: Lobsters have ten legs, including the big claws. They continue to grow throughout their lives, molting their shells many times.
Animals with more than four legs.Beetle: Beetles have six legs, and make up about a quarter of all known animal species. That makes them the most diverse group of animals.
Animals with more than four legs.Millipede: Millipedes have two pairs of legs on most segments, and one species has over 1,000 legs. They're not centipedes, and they're harmless.
Animals with more than four legs.Butterfly: Butterflies have six legs, and they taste with their feet. Landing on a plant lets them sample whether it's good for egg laying.
Animals with more than four legs.Tick: Ticks are arachnids, with eight legs as adults. They are very good at waiting, and can go for years without a meal.
Animals with more than four legs.Shrimp: Shrimp have ten legs on the main body, plus extra limbs for swimming. Some can snap claws so fast they create a shock wave.
Animals with more than four legs.Woodlouse: A land-living crustacean with seven pairs of legs. It's not an insect, and it needs damp places because it breathes with gill-like structures.
Animals with more than four legs.Grasshopper: A grasshopper has six legs, with the large back pair built for jumping. Some can leap about twenty times their body length.
Animals with more than four legs.Kangaroo: Kangaroos walk on four limbs, with the tail acting as a fifth leg. They're the only large animals to get around by hopping.
Animals with more than four legs.Snake: Snakes have no legs, though some, like boas, keep tiny hip spurs. They evolved from legged lizards.
Animals with more than four legs.Snail: A snail has a single muscular foot, not legs. It glides along on a layer of slime.
Animals with more than four legs.Earthworm: Earthworms have no legs at all, just tiny bristles called setae that grip the soil. They also have five pairs of hearts.
Animals with more than four legs.Ostrich: Two legs only, and strong ones. A single kick can seriously injure a lion.
Animals with more than four legs.Frog: Frogs have four limbs. The long back legs are built for jumping, and some species can leap more than 20 times their body length.
Animals with more than four legs.Lizard: Most lizards have four legs, though a few species, like glass lizards, have lost theirs. Some can drop a tail to escape predators.
Animals with more than four legs.Dog: Four legs, like most mammals. Dogs were domesticated from wolves at least 15,000 years ago.
Animals with more than four legs.Penguin: A two-legged bird, with flippers instead of wings. On land, it waddles, and on ice, it can toboggan on its belly.
Animals with more than four legs.Elephant: Four legs, and all of them are columns that support the weight. Elephants are among the few animals that can't jump.
Animals with more than four legs.Seal: A seal has four limbs, but they're flippers. On land, it hauls itself along on its belly or flippers.

Official Disney Princesses.Ariel: The Little Mermaid is based on Hans Christian Andersen's tale, where the original ends far more sadly. Her 1989 film revived Disney animation.
Official Disney Princesses.Belle: Belle is the only princess whose film earned a Best Picture Oscar nomination, for Beauty and the Beast in 1991. She loves books.
Official Disney Princesses.Jasmine: Jasmine is Disney's first Middle Eastern princess, from Aladdin in 1992. Her pet tiger Rajah is named from a Hindi word for king.
Official Disney Princesses.Mulan: Mulan is based on a Chinese legend, and she saves China disguised as a man. She's among the few princesses who isn't royalty by birth.
Official Disney Princesses.Pocahontas: Pocahontas was a real person, Powhatan leader's daughter, and the film changed history a lot. Real Pocahontas was a child when she met John Smith.
Official Disney Princesses.Tiana: Tiana, from The Princess and the Frog (2009), was Disney's first Black princess. She's a hardworking waitress who dreams of a restaurant.
Official Disney Princesses.Rapunzel: Her hair measures about 70 feet in Tangled, and the film cost a reported $260 million, one of the priciest animated films.
Official Disney Princesses.Merida: Merida, from Brave (2012), is Pixar's only official princess and a skilled archer who refuses an arranged marriage.
Official Disney Princesses.Moana: Moana is the daughter of a chief in Polynesia and has no love interest. Her film's songs were co-written by Lin-Manuel Miranda.
Official Disney Princesses.Aurora: Sleeping Beauty's Aurora only has about 18 minutes of screen time and speaks very few lines, far fewer than the film's fairy godmothers.
Official Disney Princesses.Cinderella: Her story is ancient, with versions from ancient Egypt to China. Disney's 1950 film saved the studio from financial trouble.
Official Disney Princesses.Snow White: Snow White (1937) was the first full-length cel-animated feature. Hollywood called it 'Disney's Folly' before it became a smash.
Official Disney Princesses.Elsa: Elsa is a queen, not an official princess, as her coronation makes her queen. Despite being a Frozen star, she isn't on the list.
Official Disney Princesses.Anna: Anna is a princess in Frozen but isn't in the official lineup. Disney keeps the franchise list restricted.
Official Disney Princesses.Fiona: Fiona is the princess in Shrek, a DreamWorks movie, and not a Disney one at all.
Official Disney Princesses.Leia: Princess Leia is a Star Wars princess. Disney owns Lucasfilm, yet she isn't in the official Disney Princess lineup.
Official Disney Princesses.Esmeralda: Esmeralda, from The Hunchback of Notre Dame, is a Romani dancer. She's not royal and not in the official lineup.
Official Disney Princesses.Wendy: Wendy Darling from Peter Pan is a girl from London. She isn't a princess, though she mothers the Lost Boys.
Official Disney Princesses.Alice: Alice from Wonderland is a curious girl, not a princess. Lewis Carroll's heroine has no royal title, though she meets a queen.
Official Disney Princesses.Dorothy: Dorothy is from The Wizard of Oz, a MGM film and not a Disney Princess. She's a farm girl from Kansas.
Official Disney Princesses.Megara: Meg from Hercules is a sharp-tongued heroine, not a princess. She isn't in the official lineup.
Official Disney Princesses.Giselle: Giselle from Enchanted (2007) is a princess in a cartoon world, but she isn't an official one.
Official Disney Princesses.Tinker Bell: Tinker Bell is a fairy. She's Disney's mascot sprinkling pixie dust, but not a princess.
Official Disney Princesses.Odette: Odette is the swan princess from The Swan Princess, a non-Disney animated film, and also in Swan Lake.

DreamWorks Animation films.Shrek: Shrek (2001) won the first Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, beating Monsters, Inc.
DreamWorks Animation films.Madagascar: Madagascar (2005) strands four zoo animals on the island, and its penguins got their own spin-off series.
DreamWorks Animation films.Kung Fu Panda: Kung Fu Panda (2008) stars Jack Black as Po, a noodle-shop panda who becomes the Dragon Warrior.
DreamWorks Animation films.Shark Tale: Shark Tale (2004) is DreamWorks' undersea comedy, with Will Smith voicing a small fish named Oscar.
DreamWorks Animation films.Megamind: Megamind (2010) flips the hero-villain formula, with a blue-headed supervillain who finally defeats his hero, Metro Man.
DreamWorks Animation films.Trolls: Trolls (2016) is based on the Good Luck Trolls dolls created by Danish woodcutter Thomas Dam, and features songs.
DreamWorks Animation films.Antz: Antz (1998) was DreamWorks' first computer-animated film, released weeks before Pixar's A Bug's Life.
DreamWorks Animation films.The Prince of Egypt: The Prince of Egypt (1998) retells Moses's story in hand-drawn animation, and its song 'When You Believe' won an Oscar.
DreamWorks Animation films.Bee Movie: Bee Movie (2007) was co-written by Jerry Seinfeld, who voices a bee who sues humans for stealing honey.
DreamWorks Animation films.The Boss Baby: The Boss Baby (2017) has Alec Baldwin voicing a briefcase-carrying baby in a suit, and earned an Oscar nomination.
DreamWorks Animation films.The Croods: The Croods (2013) follows a cave family led by Nicolas Cage, who must leave their cave in a changing world.
DreamWorks Animation films.Over the Hedge: Over the Hedge (2006) follows woodland animals confronting a suburb that appeared overnight, based on a comic strip.
DreamWorks Animation films.The Wild Robot: The Wild Robot (2024) is about a robot raised by animals on an island, with Lupita Nyong'o voicing Roz.
DreamWorks Animation films.Turbo: Turbo (2013) stars a snail who dreams of racing in the Indianapolis 500, after gaining speed powers.
DreamWorks Animation films.Toy Story: Toy Story is a Pixar film, not DreamWorks, and was the first feature-length computer-animated film.
DreamWorks Animation films.Frozen: Frozen is from Disney, not DreamWorks, and it became one of the highest-grossing animated films ever.
DreamWorks Animation films.Despicable Me: Despicable Me is from Illumination, not DreamWorks, and its Minions became hugely popular worldwide.
DreamWorks Animation films.Minions: Minions (2015) is an Illumination film, not DreamWorks, a spin-off of the Despicable Me series.
DreamWorks Animation films.Ice Age: Ice Age (2002) was made by Blue Sky Studios, not DreamWorks, and features Scrat the squirrel.
DreamWorks Animation films.Rio: Rio (2011) is a Blue Sky Studios film about a rare macaw in Brazil, and not a DreamWorks film.
DreamWorks Animation films.Cars: Cars (2006) is Pixar's world of talking vehicles, not DreamWorks, and was inspired by Route 66 road trips.
DreamWorks Animation films.Zootopia: Zootopia (2016) is a Disney film about a bunny cop, not DreamWorks, and it won the Best Animated Feature Oscar.
DreamWorks Animation films.Coraline: Coraline (2009) is a stop-motion film by Laika, not DreamWorks, based on Neil Gaiman's novella.
DreamWorks Animation films.Hotel Transylvania: Hotel Transylvania (2012) comes from Sony Pictures Animation, not DreamWorks, with Adam Sandler as Dracula.

Superheroes who can fly.Superman: Early Superman only leaped tall buildings; true flight arrived in the 1940s, partly because it was easier for animators to draw than leaping.
Superheroes who can fly.Iron Man: Tony Stark's suit flies on repulsor jets in the boots and palms, technology his comic-book self first built from scrap in a cave.
Superheroes who can fly.Storm: Ororo Munroe flies by commanding wind currents, a side effect of her weather control. She was once worshipped as a goddess in Kenya's Serengeti.
Superheroes who can fly.Captain Marvel: Carol Danvers flies by channeling cosmic energy, and her 2019 film was the first female-led solo movie in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
Superheroes who can fly.Supergirl: On Krypton, Kara Zor-El was older than baby Kal-El, but her rocket got delayed, so she landed on Earth after he was a grown hero.
Superheroes who can fly.Vision: Vision flies by manipulating his own density and gravity. In the comics, Ultron built him from the body of the android original Human Torch.
Superheroes who can fly.Green Lantern: A Green Lantern's power ring lets its wearer fly and build glowing constructs from sheer willpower, though in early comics it couldn't affect yellow things.
Superheroes who can fly.Falcon: Sam Wilson soars on mechanical wings alongside his trained bird Redwing, and he later took up Captain America's shield.
Superheroes who can fly.Martian Manhunter: J'onn J'onzz, a founding Justice League member, flies, shapeshifts and reads minds, yet his famous weakness is fire.
Superheroes who can fly.Human Torch: Johnny Storm ignites his body to fly. The name first belonged to a 1939 android hero, a different character from the Fantastic Four's Torch.
Superheroes who can fly.Hawkman: Hawkman's wings work thanks to fictional Nth metal, which defies gravity. In his lore he is a reincarnated ancient Egyptian prince.
Superheroes who can fly.Thor: Thor flies by whirling Mjolnir on its strap, but in Norse myth he traveled in a chariot pulled by two magical goats.
Superheroes who can fly.Spider-Man: Spider-Man swings on web-lines rather than flying, and in the comics his webs come from mechanical shooters he built, not his body.
Superheroes who can fly.Hulk: The Hulk can't fly, but he can leap for miles, and his huge jumps cover so much ground that they look like flight from far away.
Superheroes who can fly.Wolverine: Wolverine's healing and adamantium claws are legendary, but there's nothing in his power set that gets him off the ground.
Superheroes who can fly.The Flash: Fast enough to run across water and up walls, the Flash still runs rather than flies. Speed alone doesn't give lift.
Superheroes who can fly.Black Widow: Natasha Romanoff has no powers, only spycraft and martial skill, so when she needs to fly she needs a jet, not wings.
Superheroes who can fly.Hawkeye: Despite his bird-themed name, Clint Barton never flies. His power is an archer's aim, with trick arrows doing the rest.
Superheroes who can fly.Daredevil: Matt Murdock lost his sight but gained radar-like senses. He leaps and swings across rooftops with a billy-club cable, never flying.
Superheroes who can fly.Aquaman: Aquaman swims at tremendous speed and commands sea life, but he is earthbound on land. Flight isn't in his skill set.
Superheroes who can fly.Captain America: The super-soldier serum gave Steve Rogers peak human strength and stamina, not flight. His shield is thrown, not ridden.
Superheroes who can fly.Mr. Incredible: Bob Parr has super strength but no flight. Syndrome, the villain who envies him, needs rocket boots to get airborne.
Superheroes who can fly.Black Panther: T'Challa's heart-shaped-herb powers boost strength and agility, but flight comes from Wakandan tech like his Royal Talon Fighter.
Superheroes who can fly.Cyclops: Scott Summers fires powerful optic blasts but can't fly. His beams are so strong that ruby-quartz lenses must hold them back.

Characters in Stranger Things.Eleven: Eleven's name comes from the tattoo 011 on her wrist, and Millie Bobby Brown was only about 12 when the show started.
Characters in Stranger Things.Mike Wheeler: Mike is the Dungeon Master of the group, which explains why monsters like the Demogorgon come from Dungeons & Dragons.
Characters in Stranger Things.Dustin: Dustin has cleidocranial dysplasia, a condition actor Gaten Matarazzo also has, which the writers worked into the show.
Characters in Stranger Things.Lucas: Lucas is the party's skeptic, played by Caleb McLaughlin, who doubts Eleven and uses a wrist rocket.
Characters in Stranger Things.Will Byers: Will's disappearance into the Upside Down kicks off the series, and later he senses the monster's presence.
Characters in Stranger Things.Max: Kate Bush's 'Running Up That Hill' saves Max in season 4, sending the 1985 song to the top of the charts again.
Characters in Stranger Things.Steve Harrington: Steve starts as the school jock and ends up the group's babysitter, a character arc that fans love.
Characters in Stranger Things.Nancy: Nancy Wheeler is Mike's sister and an aspiring journalist who helps uncover the Hawkins lab's secrets.
Characters in Stranger Things.Joyce: Winona Ryder's Joyce strings Christmas lights to talk to her missing son Will in season one.
Characters in Stranger Things.Hopper: Jim Hopper is Hawkins's police chief, played by David Harbour, who is a hard-drinking loner.
Characters in Stranger Things.Robin: Robin Buckley is played by Maya Hawke, daughter of actors Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman.
Characters in Stranger Things.Vecna: Vecna's name comes from D&D's lich Vecna, an anagram of 'Vance', after fantasy author Jack Vance.
Characters in Stranger Things.Demogorgon: The Demogorgon is a D&D demon prince, and the show's monster is an actor in a suit with digital enhancements.
Characters in Stranger Things.Wednesday Addams: Wednesday is Netflix's other Jenna Ortega hit, and her 2022 dance scene went viral on TikTok.
Characters in Stranger Things.Enid Sinclair: Enid is Wednesday's werewolf roommate in Netflix's Wednesday, not part of Hawkins.
Characters in Stranger Things.Jughead Jones: Jughead is an Archie Comics character, first appearing in 1941, and Riverdale reimagined him.
Characters in Stranger Things.Archie Andrews: Archie Andrews debuted in 1941 in Archie Comics and later starred in Riverdale.
Characters in Stranger Things.Veronica Lodge: Veronica is Betty's wealthy rival for Archie's affection, a love-triangle pillar of Archie Comics and Riverdale.
Characters in Stranger Things.Pennywise: Pennywise is the dancing clown from Stephen King's It, published in 1986, set in Derry, Maine.
Characters in Stranger Things.Elliott: Elliott is the boy who befriends E.T., a film Stranger Things pays frequent homage to.
Characters in Stranger Things.Mikey Walsh: Mikey, played by Sean Astin, leads The Goonies, one of the 1980s adventure films that inspired Stranger Things.
Characters in Stranger Things.Chunk: Chunk, from The Goonies, is famous for the Truffle Shuffle, a movie that influenced the Duffer Brothers.
Characters in Stranger Things.Marty McFly: Back to the Future's Marty was first played by Eric Stoltz, who was replaced by Michael J. Fox weeks into filming.
Characters in Stranger Things.Sabrina Spellman: Sabrina the Teenage Witch debuted in Archie comics in 1962, and she's a teen, not a monster-hunter in Hawkins.

Characters in Cars.Lightning McQueen: His number 95 nods to 1995, the year Pixar's Toy Story made history as the first fully computer-animated feature.
Characters in Cars.Mater: Mater was inspired by a rusty tow truck in Galena, Kansas, on Route 66, and is voiced by Larry the Cable Guy.
Characters in Cars.Sally: Sally is a Porsche 911 Carrera who runs the Radiator Springs motel after giving up a big-city law career.
Characters in Cars.Doc Hudson: Doc is a Hudson Hornet and three-time Piston Cup winner, voiced by Paul Newman in one of his last major roles.
Characters in Cars.Luigi: Luigi is a Fiat 500 who runs a tire shop and adores Ferraris; Tony Shalhoub voices him.
Characters in Cars.Guido: Guido is a tiny forklift who can change four tires in seconds and speaks mostly Italian.
Characters in Cars.Ramone: Ramone is a 1959 Chevy Impala lowrider who repaints himself every day, and he runs the custom paint shop.
Characters in Cars.Flo: Flo is a 1957 Motorama show car who runs the V8 Cafe and is married to Ramone.
Characters in Cars.Fillmore: Fillmore is a VW bus hippie, originally voiced by George Carlin, who sells his own organic fuel.
Characters in Cars.Sarge: Sarge is a military Jeep and neighbor of Fillmore, who raises the flag and plays reveille every morning.
Characters in Cars.Chick Hicks: The green rival with a mustache-like grille is a Buick, and he would do anything to win the Piston Cup.
Characters in Cars.The King: Strip Weathers is a No. 43 Plymouth Superbird, voiced by racing legend Richard Petty, who is the real-life King.
Characters in Cars.Mack: Mack is the Mack truck who hauls McQueen to races, and he falls asleep on the road at the start of the story.
Characters in Cars.Cruz Ramirez: Cruz is a trainer turned racer in Cars 3, and she is voiced by Cristela Alonzo.
Characters in Cars.Thomas: Thomas is a tank engine, not a car, and he first appeared in the Rev. W. Awdry's 1945 Railway Series books.
Characters in Cars.Percy: Percy is a small green tank engine in Thomas's world; no cars and no Radiator Springs.
Characters in Cars.Gordon: Gordon is a big blue express engine in the Thomas stories, who is not from Cars.
Characters in Cars.Bumblebee: Bumblebee is a Transformer who turns into a Camaro, from a different franchise altogether.
Characters in Cars.Optimus Prime: Optimus Prime is the leader of the Autobots and shapeshifts into a truck in the Transformers films.
Characters in Cars.Herbie: Herbie is a Volkswagen Beetle with racing number 53 who first drove into theaters in 1968's The Love Bug.
Characters in Cars.KITT: KITT is a talking black Pontiac Trans Am from the TV series Knight Rider, not from the Cars films.
Characters in Cars.Turbo: Turbo is a snail who dreams of the Indy 500 in his own DreamWorks movie, not Cars.
Characters in Cars.Speed Racer: Speed Racer drives the Mach Five in a 1960s Japanese anime, not Cars, though both star racers.
Characters in Cars.Scoop: Scoop is Bob the Builder's yellow backhoe, from a different kids' series about machines.

Minecraft mobs.Creeper: It came from a bug while Notch was making a pig model; the creeper's tall shape resulted from mixing up the dimensions.
Minecraft mobs.Zombie: Burns in sunlight, and can break wooden doors on harder difficulties.
Minecraft mobs.Skeleton: The archer mob also burns in daylight, and its arrows can sometimes kill a creeper, causing it to drop a music disc.
Minecraft mobs.Enderman: Teleports and gets angry if you look it in the eye; water hurts it.
Minecraft mobs.Ghast: A floating, crying creature in the Nether whose fireballs can be reflected back to kill it.
Minecraft mobs.Blaze: A Nether mob that drops blaze rods, essential for brewing potions and finding the End.
Minecraft mobs.Wither: A boss summoned by building a T of soul sand with three skulls; it's the only way to get a Nether star.
Minecraft mobs.Villager: Trades with emeralds and has a profession by its workstation; a zombie villager can be cured with a golden apple.
Minecraft mobs.Piglin: A pig-like Nether mob that loves gold, and gets angry if you don't wear any golden armor.
Minecraft mobs.Warden: A blind deep-dark guardian that hunts by sound and vibrations, added in the 1.19 Wild Update.
Minecraft mobs.Slime: A cube that splits into smaller ones when killed; they spawn in swamps and certain chunks underground.
Minecraft mobs.Axolotl: Based on a real salamander, a Minecraft axolotl can play dead and helps fight aquatic mobs.
Minecraft mobs.Goomba: A Mario enemy, from a different game, not Minecraft.
Minecraft mobs.Koopa: A walking turtle from Mario games, and nothing like Minecraft's mobs, though the game does have turtles of its own.
Minecraft mobs.Boo: A Mario ghost, not a Minecraft mob; Minecraft's ghosts are phantoms.
Minecraft mobs.Octorok: A rock-spitting octopus from Zelda, not Minecraft.
Minecraft mobs.Moblin: A pig-faced goblin of Zelda, not part of Minecraft, though Piglins are similar.
Minecraft mobs.Chocobo: A rideable bird in Final Fantasy, unrelated to Minecraft's chickens.
Minecraft mobs.Pikachu: The Pokemon mascot, not in Minecraft vanilla, despite mods that add it.
Minecraft mobs.Bokoblin: A Zelda enemy in Breath of the Wild, not Minecraft.
Minecraft mobs.Cacodemon: A floating red demon from Doom, not Minecraft's.
Minecraft mobs.Shy Guy: A masked Mario enemy, not a Minecraft mob.
Minecraft mobs.Metroid: A floating jellyfish-like parasite from Nintendo's series, not Minecraft.

Objects from Greek mythology.Golden Fleece: The prize of Jason's quest hung from a tree guarded by a sleepless dragon in Colchis.
Objects from Greek mythology.Trojan Horse: The Greeks hid warriors inside a giant wooden horse to end a ten-year siege; Homer's Odyssey mentions it, though the Iliad stops before it.
Objects from Greek mythology.Pandora's box: In Greek, it was a jar, not a box; the jar's evils escaped and only hope stayed inside, so it was mistranslated by Erasmus.
Objects from Greek mythology.Aegis: Athena's protective shield or cloak, bearing Medusa's head; 'under the aegis of' still means under protection.
Objects from Greek mythology.Trident: The three-pronged spear of Poseidon, said to shake the earth and whip up storms; it's likely derived from a fisherman's fish-spear.
Objects from Greek mythology.Caduceus: Hermes's staff with two snakes and wings; it's often confused with the single-snake rod of Asclepius that is the true medical symbol.
Objects from Greek mythology.Ambrosia: Food of the gods that kept them immortal; its name comes from a Greek word meaning 'not mortal'.
Objects from Greek mythology.Golden apple: Eris's apple, marked 'for the fairest', led to the Judgment of Paris, and thus to the Trojan War.
Objects from Greek mythology.Ariadne's thread: The ball of thread she gave Theseus let him escape the Labyrinth; today it means a way out of a problem.
Objects from Greek mythology.Helm of Darkness: Hades's helmet of invisibility, lent to Perseus and Athena so they could slip past foes unseen.
Objects from Greek mythology.Excalibur: A trap: King Arthur's sword is from British legend, not Greek myth.
Objects from Greek mythology.Mjolnir: A trap: Thor's hammer is Norse and always returns to his hand after being thrown.
Objects from Greek mythology.Holy Grail: A trap: the chalice of Arthurian legend, tied to the Last Supper, is not a Greek relic.
Objects from Greek mythology.Gungnir: A trap: Odin's Norse spear never misses its target, and so isn't from Greek myth.
Objects from Greek mythology.Round Table: A trap: King Arthur's table, made so no knight sat above another, is not Greek.
Objects from Greek mythology.Philosopher's stone: A medieval alchemy goal, said to turn lead into gold, meant to grant immortality; European not Greek.
Objects from Greek mythology.Brisingamen: Freya's Norse necklace, which she earned by spending a night with each of four dwarves.
Objects from Greek mythology.Draupnir: A trap: Odin's ring drips eight new gold rings every ninth night, and is Norse, not Greek.
Objects from Greek mythology.Aladdin's lamp: A Middle Eastern tale from the Arabian Nights, which actually was added by a French translator.
Objects from Greek mythology.Magic carpet: A trap: it comes from Arabian and Persian tales, not Greek myth.
Objects from Greek mythology.Glass slipper: Cinderella's footwear from French fairy tales by Perrault; some scholars think it came from a translation error of fur.
Objects from Greek mythology.Sword in the stone: A trap: the Arthurian proof of the rightful king is British legend, not Greek myth.
Objects from Greek mythology.Seven-league boots: From French fairy tales such as Perrault's Hop o' My Thumb, each step covered seven leagues, around 20 miles.
Objects from Greek mythology.Gjallarhorn: A trap: Heimdall's Norse horn, to be blown at Ragnarok, is not Greek.

Cities founded by the Romans.London: Founded as Londinium around AD 43 after Claudius's invasion, and Boudica's rebels burned it down around AD 60.
Cities founded by the Romans.Florence: Founded as Florentia around 59 BC as a colony for veterans, laid out on a neat Roman grid.
Cities founded by the Romans.Cologne: Founded as Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, named for Agrippina, hence 'Cologne' from the Latin colonia.
Cities founded by the Romans.York: Eboracum was a major fortress, and Constantine was proclaimed emperor here in AD 306.
Cities founded by the Romans.Chester: Began as the legionary fortress Deva, and the 'chester' ending comes from the Latin castra, camp.
Cities founded by the Romans.Bath: Aquae Sulis grew around hot springs and a temple to Sulis Minerva, and the baths still survive.
Cities founded by the Romans.Zaragoza: Founded as Caesaraugusta for Emperor Augustus, and Zaragoza is a worn-down form of the name.
Cities founded by the Romans.Lyon: Lugdunum was capital of Gaul, and emperors Claudius and Caracalla were both born here.
Cities founded by the Romans.Mainz: Mogontiacum was a legion base on the Rhine, and Gutenberg was born here, the printing press pioneer.
Cities founded by the Romans.Gloucester: Glevum began as a colony for retired legionaries around AD 97, and the name Gloucester descends from it.
Cities founded by the Romans.Athens: The Greeks of Athens founded it themselves long before Rome mattered; its roots are in a Mycenaean citadel.
Cities founded by the Romans.Marseille: Greeks from Phocaea founded it about 600 BC, making it France's oldest city.
Cities founded by the Romans.Naples: Greek colonists founded Neapolis, meaning 'new city', centuries before Rome conquered it.
Cities founded by the Romans.Istanbul: Founded as Byzantium by Greeks around 660 BC; Constantine refounded it in AD 330, so Romans rebuilt rather than founded it.
Cities founded by the Romans.Cadiz: Phoenician traders founded Gadir around 1100 BC, making it one of western Europe's oldest cities.
Cities founded by the Romans.Alexandria: Alexander the Great founded it in 331 BC; the Romans took it over after Cleopatra.
Cities founded by the Romans.Moscow: A medieval city first recorded in 1147, so the Romans never knew it.
Cities founded by the Romans.Venice: Traditionally founded in AD 421 by refugees fleeing invaders, not by Roman settlers.
Cities founded by the Romans.Amsterdam: It began as a fishing village around a dam on the Amstel in the 1200s, long after Rome's fall.
Cities founded by the Romans.Madrid: It was founded in the 9th century as a Muslim fortress called Mayrit, not by the Romans.
Cities founded by the Romans.Berlin: A medieval market town from the 1200s on the Spree, never a Roman colony.
Cities founded by the Romans.Edinburgh: The Romans built the Antonine Wall across Scotland, but Edinburgh grew from an Iron Age hillfort.
Cities founded by the Romans.Syracuse: Corinthian Greeks founded it in 734 BC, and Archimedes lived here.
Cities founded by the Romans.Oslo: Tradition credits King Harald Hardrada with founding it around 1049, centuries after Rome's end.

Objects that have legs.Table: Many designs have four legs for stability, but a three-legged table never wobbles on uneven floors, because three points always define a plane.
Objects that have legs.Chair: Most have four legs, though the oldest known chairs were Egyptian, and some of them had animal-shaped legs like lion paws.
Objects that have legs.Stool: A seat with legs but no back, and three-legged ones suit uneven ground, which is why milking stools often have three.
Objects that have legs.Tripod: Three legs make the most stable support on uneven ground, and it's the standard for cameras and surveying instruments.
Objects that have legs.Easel: A stand with three legs that holds a canvas, and it sets the painting at the best angle for the artist.
Objects that have legs.Grand piano: Typically three sturdy legs support its heavy frame, and a concert grand can weigh over 500 kilograms.
Objects that have legs.Ironing board: Its folding legs form an X for storage, and the scissor structure lets the board be easily adjusted for height.
Objects that have legs.Desk: The Resolute desk in the Oval Office was carved from the timbers of HMS Resolute, an Arctic ship, and given to the US by Queen Victoria in 1880.
Objects that have legs.Bench: A seat with legs for several people, and courts are often called 'the bench' for the long seat on which judges once sat.
Objects that have legs.Trousers: Each leg has its own tube, and the word trousers is always plural. Ancient trousers have been found on a Chinese mummy of about 3,000 years ago.
Objects that have legs.Drawing compass: Two jointed legs, one with a point and one with a pencil, let you draw perfect circles, and the tool has been used since antiquity.
Objects that have legs.Bunk bed: Two beds stacked on a shared frame, and the legs of the structure serve as support. It was developed for ships and barracks where space was tight.
Objects that have legs.Rug: Trap: it lies flat on the floor with no legs, and the oldest known knotted carpet, Pazyryk, is over 2,000 years old.
Objects that have legs.Hand mirror: Trap: this is a handle and glass, with no legs, though a stand version would have a base.
Objects that have legs.Curtain: Trap: it hangs from a rail and has no legs.
Objects that have legs.Pillow: Trap: it is stuffed with feathers or foam and no legs, though it might be on a bed that has them.
Objects that have legs.Bean bag: Trap: it is a sack of beads and conforms to your shape with no legs, and was first sold in Italy in the 1960s.
Objects that have legs.Hammock: Trap: it hangs between two points and has no legs, though a hammock stand would add them.
Objects that have legs.Vase: Trap: it sits on a flat base and has no legs.
Objects that have legs.Wall clock: Trap: it hangs from a nail and has no legs, though a grandfather clock stands on feet.
Objects that have legs.Doormat: Trap: it lies flat with no legs and is only meant for wiping feet.
Objects that have legs.Blanket: Trap: a flat sheet of fabric with no legs.
Objects that have legs.Picture frame: Trap: some have a small fold-out support at the back, but not legs, and it usually hangs on a wall.
Objects that have legs.Bucket: Trap: it has a handle and a base, but no legs.

Things usually made of glass.Window: Window glass is made mostly from sand, and the float process, invented in the 1950s, gives panes their flat, smooth finish.
Things usually made of glass.Wine glass: Crystal glass contains lead oxide or substitutes, which raises its sparkle and makes it ring when you flick the rim.
Things usually made of glass.Mirror: A mirror is glass with a thin metal coating on the back, usually silver or aluminum, which does the actual reflecting.
Things usually made of glass.Light bulb: The 'Centennial Light' in a California fire station has been glowing, almost nonstop, since about 1901.
Things usually made of glass.Jam jar: Glass doesn't absorb flavors or smells, which is why jars are so good at preserving food.
Things usually made of glass.Marble: Glass marbles became popular in the 1800s once a German glassblower invented a tool to make them in bulk.
Things usually made of glass.Vase: Murano, near Venice, has been famous for glassmaking since 1291, when the furnaces were moved there to avoid fire risk.
Things usually made of glass.Snow globe: The first snow globe is credited to an Austrian maker in the 1800s, and early 'snow' was made from ground rice or bone.
Things usually made of glass.Eyeglass lens: Most modern lenses are plastic now, but glass lenses scratch less, which is why some people still prefer them.
Things usually made of glass.Test tube: Lab test tubes use borosilicate glass, which resists heat and sudden temperature changes better than ordinary glass.
Things usually made of glass.Fish bowl: Round fish bowls are often considered poor homes, since the small surface limits oxygen and fish can't swim far.
Things usually made of glass.Hourglass: Sand timers have been used at sea since at least the 1300s because waves don't throw them off like a clock.
Things usually made of glass.Mug: A trap: most mugs are ceramic, which is made from fired clay, not molten sand like glass.
Things usually made of glass.Spoon: Spoons are usually metal, wood, or plastic, and a glass spoon would be too brittle for stirring hot food.
Things usually made of glass.Brick: Bricks are fired clay, not glass, though extreme heat can melt sand into glass, as in some lightning strikes.
Things usually made of glass.Teapot: Most teapots are ceramic or metal, though glass versions exist for watching the leaves unfurl.
Things usually made of glass.Candle: A candle is wax and wick, though glass jars often hold them, and the glass shouldn't be mistaken for the candle.
Things usually made of glass.Plate: Most plates are ceramic or porcelain, and porcelain was so prized in Europe that it was nicknamed 'white gold'.
Things usually made of glass.Sponge: Natural sponges are animals, simple creatures that have lived on the sea floor for over 500 million years.
Things usually made of glass.Pillow: Pillows are filled with feathers or foam and wrapped in cloth, nothing hard, brittle, or breakable.
Things usually made of glass.Coin: Coins are metal, and modern ones are often copper-nickel or steel; glass would shatter in a pocket.
Things usually made of glass.Pencil: The 'lead' is actually graphite mixed with clay, wrapped in wood, with no glass at all.
Things usually made of glass.Shoe: Shoes are leather, fabric, or rubber; glass shoes would shatter, so Cinderella's glass slipper is best left to fairy tales.
Things usually made of glass.Feather: Feathers are made of keratin, the same protein as your nails, light, flexible, and nothing like brittle glass.

Things that give off light.Desk lamp: The Anglepoise lamp, patented in 1932, used springs to hold any position, and the design is still copied.
Things that give off light.Chandelier: Early chandeliers held candles, and a grand one could take servants hours to light.
Things that give off light.Candle: A candle flame glows because tiny soot particles in it get hot enough to shine.
Things that give off light.Flashlight: The flashlight emerged around 1899 from a battery and bulb in a tube, and early ones were sold as novelties.
Things that give off light.Ceiling light: Light fittings on the ceiling spread light downward, and a bright one can be about as bright as 800 candles.
Things that give off light.Night light: Night lights are often dim and warm-toned because bright or blue light can disturb sleep.
Things that give off light.Lantern: The oldest lanterns burned oil and had a shield of horn or glass, and Chinese paper lanterns are celebrated in festivals.
Things that give off light.Fairy lights: The first string of electric Christmas lights appeared in 1882, designed by Edward Johnson, an Edison associate.
Things that give off light.Lava lamp: Edward Craven Walker invented it in 1963 after seeing a homemade egg timer of wax floating in liquid in a pub.
Things that give off light.Floor lamp: A floor lamp casts light from a stand, and a tall one lights a room softly from above.
Things that give off light.Wall sconce: Sconces began as candle holders on castle walls, and the name derives from an old French word for a lantern.
Things that give off light.Neon sign: Neon glows red-orange, and other colors come from other gases or from coatings on the tube.
Things that give off light.Mirror: A mirror reflects light but makes none of its own, which is why a dark room stays dark even with one.
Things that give off light.Lampshade: A lampshade only diffuses light from the bulb, and it isn't a source of its own.
Things that give off light.Window: A window lets sunlight in, but at night it gives off nothing, so it fails the 'gives off light' test.
Things that give off light.Skylight: A skylight lets daylight through the roof, but it doesn't produce any light itself.
Things that give off light.Curtains: Curtains block or filter light, and blackout versions stop nearly all of it.
Things that give off light.Blinds: Blinds control how much light enters, and they've been in use since ancient Egypt in some form.
Things that give off light.Light switch: A switch just controls the circuit, and the glow comes from the bulb it turns on.
Things that give off light.Dimmer switch: A dimmer reduces power to the bulb, so it controls light and doesn't produce it.
Things that give off light.Picture frame: A picture frame holds art, though some modern ones have backlights.
Things that give off light.Prism: A prism splits white light into colors, as Isaac Newton showed in the 1660s, but it makes no light of its own.
Things that give off light.Glass vase: A glass vase can catch and bend light, but it won't glow by itself.
Things that give off light.Sunglasses: Sunglasses reduce light reaching your eyes, and early Chinese versions used smoky quartz in the 1100s.

Things you might see on a roof.Chimney: Santa isn't the only one climbing down chimneys: chimney sweeps once ran a huge trade, and a flue fire can burn above 2,000 degrees.
Things you might see on a roof.Shingles: Asphalt shingles cover most American homes, and they come in 'three tab' style or thicker laminated ones that last decades.
Things you might see on a roof.Skylight: Skylights bring in daylight through the roof, and a roof window can flood a room with up to several times more light than a wall window.
Things you might see on a roof.Solar panels: Solar panels work in cold, sunny weather even better than hot, because very high temperatures actually lower their efficiency.
Things you might see on a roof.Satellite dish: A dish must be aimed at a satellite in geostationary orbit, roughly 22,000 miles above the equator, which is why it points at the southern sky in the US.
Things you might see on a roof.TV aerial: The classic H-shaped TV aerial works because its rod lengths are matched to the wavelength of broadcast signals.
Things you might see on a roof.Weather vane: Weather vanes point toward where the wind is coming from, and many are shaped like roosters, a tradition from medieval times.
Things you might see on a roof.Roof tiles: Clay roof tiles have been used for thousands of years, and some ancient Roman tiles are still doing their job today.
Things you might see on a roof.Dormer window: A dormer is a small structure sticking out of a sloped roof with its own window; it gives attic rooms light and headroom.
Things you might see on a roof.Lightning rod: Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod in the 1750s; it doesn't attract strikes, it gives them a safe path to ground.
Things you might see on a roof.Doormat: A doormat is by the door at ground level, so it's among the few things in a home that is nowhere near the roof.
Things you might see on a roof.Mailbox: A mailbox sits on the street or wall, and in the US it's federal property, so only the postal service may put mail in.
Things you might see on a roof.Front door: The front door is at ground level, and the average one is around 80 inches tall by 36 inches wide.
Things you might see on a roof.Patio: A patio is a paved outdoor space beside the house, and the word came from Spanish, where it means an inner courtyard.
Things you might see on a roof.Doorbell: The doorbell is by the door at ground level, and the first electric ones appeared in the 1800s.
Things you might see on a roof.Garage door: The garage door is a big part of the front of many homes, and electric openers became common in the 1960s.
Things you might see on a roof.Driveway: The driveway lies on the ground beside the house, so it's about as far from the roof as you can get.
Things you might see on a roof.Lawn: The lawn is at ground level; American lawns cover an area bigger than the state of Georgia by some estimates.
Things you might see on a roof.Fence: A fence marks the boundary at ground level, and one in Australia, the Dingo Fence, runs about 3,400 miles.
Things you might see on a roof.Basement: The basement is the opposite of the roof, the lowest level of the house, partly or fully underground.
Things you might see on a roof.Porch steps: Porch steps are at ground level, and building codes often limit how tall each step may be.
Things you might see on a roof.Sump pump: A sump pump sits in a pit in the basement and pushes water out to keep the home from flooding.
Things you might see on a roof.Flower bed: A flower bed is a garden feature on the ground, and its ancestors were the formal beds of 1600s French gardens.
Things you might see on a roof.Sidewalk: The sidewalk is in front of the house at street level, and the first ones were made in ancient Roman cities.

Words for feeling tired.Sleepy: The sleepiest time of day for most people is in the mid-afternoon, around 2 to 4 pm, because of a natural dip in body temperature.
Words for feeling tired.Drowsy: Drowsy driving causes tens of thousands of crashes yearly, and being awake for 18 hours impairs you like a blood alcohol level of 0.05.
Words for feeling tired.Exhausted: Exhausted comes from Latin exhaurire, to draw out, and it literally means emptied, like a well that has been drained.
Words for feeling tired.Weary: Weary dates back to Old English, and it can mean tired of something, like being weary of waiting.
Words for feeling tired.Fatigued: Fatigue is also used in engineering, where metal fatigue can make an airplane part crack after repeated stress.
Words for feeling tired.Knackered: Knackered is British slang, and a knacker once was a person who bought worn-out horses and slaughtered them for parts.
Words for feeling tired.Pooped: Pooped may come from the poop deck of a ship, where a wave smashing over the stern could leave a crew soaked and exhausted.
Words for feeling tired.Beat: Beat meaning tired is American slang from the 1800s, and the Beat Generation writers used it for being worn down.
Words for feeling tired.Drained: Drained suggests a battery emptying, and it fits, since our brains use about 20 percent of the body's energy.
Words for feeling tired.Worn out: Worn out comes from cloth and clothing that wears thin, a fitting image for a person at the end of a long day.
Words for feeling tired.Bushed: Bushed is thought to have come from lumberjacks and trappers who had spent too long in the bush, getting lost and weary.
Words for feeling tired.Groggy: Groggy comes from grog, the watered rum sailors drank, and it described the sluggishness of someone who had a little too much.
Words for feeling tired.Spent: Spent is used for money and for energy: if you have spent all you have, you are exhausted, as with a spent bullet.
Words for feeling tired.Alert: Alert comes from the Italian all'erta, which means on the watch, and soldiers used it long before anyone was caffeinated.
Words for feeling tired.Wired: Wired means the opposite of tired: jittery and hyper, often after too much caffeine, which blocks the sleepy signals in your brain.
Words for feeling tired.Peppy: Peppy comes from pep, short for pepper, which suggested sharp energy, and it means lively, not tired.
Words for feeling tired.Energetic: Energetic comes from the Greek energeia, which means activity, and it is the opposite of weary.
Words for feeling tired.Lively: Lively once meant living, and it still shows in the word's roots, meaning full of life, the opposite of tired.
Words for feeling tired.Perky: Perky originally meant jaunty or proud, and a perky person is cheerful and spirited, not worn out.
Words for feeling tired.Refreshed: Refreshed is what you feel after a full sleep cycle, which lasts about 90 minutes and repeats several times a night.
Words for feeling tired.Wide awake: Wide awake is a true opposite of sleepy, and the phrase has been used since the 1700s for being fully alert.
Words for feeling tired.Rested: Rested is the opposite of tired, and a good night of sleep also helps your brain sweep away waste products.
Words for feeling tired.Hyper: Hyper is short for hyperactive, which is the opposite of tired, even though kids can get hyper when they are overtired.
Words for feeling tired.Chipper: Chipper is a cheerful word that means lively and in good spirits, so it is the opposite of drowsy.

Things that are scary at 3am.Creaking floor: Houses creak at night when wood contracts as it cools, but it still sounds exactly like footsteps.
Things that are scary at 3am.Footsteps: With nothing else to hear at night, small sounds seem louder, and even ordinary footsteps can feel menacing.
Things that are scary at 3am.Doorbell: A doorbell at 3am instantly makes you wonder who would visit at that hour, which is exactly why it's unnerving.
Things that are scary at 3am.Scratching noise: Scratching in the walls is often mice or rats, and the quiet of the night makes them easy to hear.
Things that are scary at 3am.Phone ringing: Calls in the middle of the night are rarely good news, so your brain assumes the worst before you're even awake.
Things that are scary at 3am.Whispering: Whispers are creepier than shouts because your brain strains to decode them, and the unknown unsettles us.
Things that are scary at 3am.Shadow figure: Seeing figures in shadows is pareidolia, the brain's habit of finding faces and people in random patterns.
Things that are scary at 3am.Knock at the door: A knock in the dead of night is a classic horror trope, and it still sends your heart racing.
Things that are scary at 3am.Clown doll: Dolls tap the uncanny valley: figures that look almost human but not quite, which the brain finds unsettling.
Things that are scary at 3am.Smoke alarm: Smoke alarms often start chirping at night, when a cooler house weakens the battery just enough to trigger the low-battery warning.
Things that are scary at 3am.Creepy laughter: Unexplained laughter in the night is the stuff of horror films, since laughter is normally social.
Things that are scary at 3am.Glowing eyes: Many animals' eyes glow in the dark thanks to the tapetum lucidum, a reflective layer that boosts night vision.
Things that are scary at 3am.Unknown caller: An unknown caller at 3am may just be a wrong number, but in horror it's a classic because you can't know who's on the line.
Things that are scary at 3am.Rainbow: A rainbow is really a full circle, but from the ground we usually see only an arc, and it's a daytime joy.
Things that are scary at 3am.Birthday cake: The tradition of birthday candles may date from the ancient Greeks, who offered round cakes with candles to Artemis.
Things that are scary at 3am.Butterfly: Butterflies taste with their feet, and as daytime fliers they're gentle visitors, rarely seen at your window at night.
Things that are scary at 3am.Sunflower: Young sunflowers follow the sun across the sky, a behavior called heliotropism, so they symbolize daytime cheer.
Things that are scary at 3am.Bubble bath: Bubbles last because soap makes water films stretchy and tough, so a bubble bath is relaxing, not scary.
Things that are scary at 3am.Ice cream: Ice cream is a joy at any hour; at 3am it's a guilty-pleasure raid on the freezer.
Things that are scary at 3am.Lunch break: Lunch is a midday event, which couldn't be further from the dead of night.
Things that are scary at 3am.Beach day: Beach days are bright and warm, while at 3am the beach would be dark and cold.
Things that are scary at 3am.Picnic: Picnics are made for daylight, and the word comes from French pique-nique, a meal where guests brought their own food.
Things that are scary at 3am.Lemonade: Lemonade is a classic summer drink, and a lemonade stand is one of the most traditional childhood businesses.
Things that are scary at 3am.Bunny slippers: Bunny slippers are cute and comforting, the one thing that makes a 3am walk to the kitchen less scary.

Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Smartphone: The first smartphone arrived in 1994 (IBM Simon), but the modern touchscreen kind came with the iPhone in 2007.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Airplane: The Wright brothers flew in 1903, so in 1826 no one had flown, apart from hot-air balloon pioneers.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Television: Television appeared in the 1920s, and John Logie Baird demonstrated a working version in 1926.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Light bulb: The practical light bulb arrived around 1879 with Thomas Edison and Joseph Swan, though arc lamps predate it.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Car: Karl Benz patented the first practical gas car in 1886; steam-powered road vehicles were crawling about before that, though.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Plastic bag: Plastic bags came in the 1960s, and the one-piece polyethylene shopping bag took over in the 1970s and 80s.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Internet: The internet grew from ARPANET in the 1960s, and the web came in 1989 and 1991.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Radio: Radio waves were demonstrated in the 1880s, and Marconi sent signals across the Atlantic in 1901.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Microwave: The microwave oven was developed by Percy Spencer, a radar engineer, in the 1940s.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell's telephone patent came in 1876, half a century too late for 1826.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Movie theater: Movie theaters arrived in the 1890s, after Lumiere brothers' 1895 public film show in Paris.
