Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Zipper: The modern zipper was developed in the 1890s and 1910s, and in 1926 it wasn't yet common on clothes.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Vacuum cleaner: The vacuum cleaner came around 1901, when Hubert Cecil Booth built a huge horse-drawn one in London.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Candle: Candles are ancient, and the Romans made them from tallow before 1826 and 200 years ago, too.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Horse carriage: Horse carriages were the main transport in the 1820s, so their boom had peaked long before.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Book: Books were centuries old by then, as Gutenberg's press dates to about 1450.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Violin: The violin took shape in 16th-century Italy, and Stradivari's famous instruments date from around 1700.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Wig: Wigs were common long before 1826, though the powdered fashion had faded since the French Revolution.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Bread: Bread is thousands of years old, and the oldest known remains of bread date back about 14,000 years.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Sailing ship: Sailing ships were at their peak, and the age of sail was still going strong in the 1820s.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Quill pen: Quill pens were the standard writing tool, and steel pens only took over in the mid-1800s.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Telescope: Telescopes date to around 1608 in the Netherlands, and Galileo improved on them in 1609.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Clock: Mechanical clocks existed since the 1300s, and pendulum clocks since Huygens in 1656.
Things that didn't exist 200 years ago.Piano: Pianos were invented around 1700 by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Florence, and Beethoven wrote for them.

Jobs that treat human patients.Surgeon: The first successful anesthesia used in a surgery was in the 1840s, which changed the job from a race against pain to careful work.
Jobs that treat human patients.Nurse: Florence Nightingale made nursing a professional career in the 1800s, and her data on hospital hygiene saved many lives.
Jobs that treat human patients.Anesthesiologist: Anesthesiologists keep patients asleep and safe during surgery, and many call it constant vigilance with moments of drama.
Jobs that treat human patients.Midwife: Midwives help with births, and the word means "with woman" in Old English, and the profession is among the world's oldest.
Jobs that treat human patients.Pediatrician: Pediatricians treat children, and a baby's dosage is based on weight because kids are not just small adults.
Jobs that treat human patients.Cardiologist: Cardiologists treat the heart, which beats about 100,000 times a day in an average adult.
Jobs that treat human patients.Dermatologist: Skin is the body's largest organ, and a dermatologist treats everything from acne to skin cancer.
Jobs that treat human patients.Paramedic: Paramedics give emergency care on the way to the hospital, where the early minutes after an injury can matter greatly.
Jobs that treat human patients.Optometrist: Optometrists test eyesight and prescribe glasses, but they are not surgeons, unlike ophthalmologists.
Jobs that treat human patients.Oncologist: Oncologists treat cancer, and the name comes from the Greek onkos, meaning mass or lump.
Jobs that treat human patients.Dentist: Dentists treat people's teeth, and enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
Jobs that treat human patients.Veterinarian: Veterinarians treat animals, not people, so they don't fit even though they're also medical experts.
Jobs that treat human patients.Astrologer: Astrology claims stars shape our lives, but there's no scientific evidence, so an astrologer isn't a healthcare provider.
Jobs that treat human patients.Astronomer: Astronomers study the stars and planets, and not patients.
Jobs that treat human patients.Geologist: Geologists study rocks and the Earth, so there's no patient involved.
Jobs that treat human patients.Archaeologist: Archaeologists study the human past through remains, and the only "patients" are old bones.
Jobs that treat human patients.Meteorologist: Meteorologists forecast the weather, so they treat storms, not people.
Jobs that treat human patients.Sociologist: Sociologists study societies and group behavior, not individual patients.
Jobs that treat human patients.Paleontologist: Paleontologists study fossils and ancient life, and their subjects have been dead millions of years.
Jobs that treat human patients.Ornithologist: Ornithologists study birds in the wild, and the name comes from the Greek ornis for bird, so no human patients here.
Jobs that treat human patients.Etymologist: Etymologists study word origins, and the similar-sounding entomologists study insects, but neither treats patients.
Jobs that treat human patients.Seismologist: Seismologists study earthquakes, so their subject is the Earth.
Jobs that treat human patients.Anthropologist: Anthropologists study human cultures and origins, but they don't treat illness.
Jobs that treat human patients.Numerologist: Numerology claims numbers hold hidden meaning, with no scientific basis, and it isn't medical treatment.

Building materials.Brick: Fired clay bricks have been used for over 5,000 years, and some Roman walls still stand.
Building materials.Concrete: Roman concrete used volcanic ash, and the Pantheon's dome remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
Building materials.Timber: Timber is making a comeback: modern wooden towers now rise over 80 meters.
Building materials.Steel: Steel framing made skyscrapers possible, beginning with Chicago's Home Insurance Building in 1885.
Building materials.Glass: Mostly made from sand, glass can be recycled endlessly without losing quality.
Building materials.Plaster: Plaster of Paris is named for the gypsum once quarried near Paris, and it warms as it hardens.
Building materials.Drywall: Plasterboard was patented in 1894 by Augustine Sackett and took off after World War II.
Building materials.Cement: Cement is the binding powder in concrete, and its production causes roughly 8 percent of global CO2.
Building materials.Mortar: Old lime mortar is softer than the bricks, so it takes the damage first and can be repaired.
Building materials.Gravel: Gravel and sand make up most of concrete's volume, typically about three quarters.
Building materials.Tile: Fired-clay roof tiles have covered buildings in China and Greece for thousands of years.
Building materials.Insulation: Fiberglass insulation was discovered by accident in 1932 when a jet of compressed air hit molten glass.
Building materials.Rebar: Steel bars work inside concrete because steel and concrete expand at almost the same rate.
Building materials.Silk: Spun by silkworms, silk is a fabric, and for its weight a spider's silk can outmatch steel.
Building materials.Velvet: A soft fabric whose name probably comes from the Latin villus, meaning shaggy hair.
Building materials.Denim: The name comes from serge de Nimes, a fabric made in Nimes, France.
Building materials.Jelly: A wobbly dessert in Britain, but in the US the word means fruit spread.
Building materials.Marzipan: Almond paste used in cakes and candies, so it is edible, not structural.
Building materials.Feathers: Feathers insulate birds and jackets, thanks to trapped air, but no one builds a house from them.
Building materials.Lace: Delicate openwork cloth, with bobbin lace once a luxury industry in places like Bruges and Nottingham.
Building materials.Satin: Satin is a type of weave, not a fiber, so it can be made of silk or polyester.
Building materials.Cashmere: It takes the wool of several goats to make a single sweater.
Building materials.Chiffon: A sheer fabric whose name comes from the French for rag.
Building materials.Tinsel: Christmas tinsel was once made from real silver, then lead, and now plastic.

Jobs in ancient Egypt.Scribe: Scribes were among the most respected workers, since reading and writing were rare, and they trained for years in hieroglyphs.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Embalmer: Embalmers removed organs, dried the body in natron salt for about 40 days, and wrapped it in linen to preserve it for the afterlife.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Priest: Priests bathed, shaved and dressed the god's statue each day, since the temple was considered the god's home.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Vizier: The vizier was the pharaoh's chief minister, similar to a prime minister, and oversaw justice, taxes and building projects.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Farmer: Most Egyptians farmed along the Nile, whose yearly flood left fertile black silt that made the land so rich.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Potter: Potters made pots, jars and cooking vessels, using a wheel from around the Old Kingdom, and their work is a gift for archaeologists.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Stonemason: Skilled masons cut and shaped the blocks for temples and pyramids, using copper tools and sand to polish stone.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Brewer: Beer was a daily staple, even for workers, and pyramid builders were partly paid in beer rations.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Baker: Bakers made bread, the staple food, and emmer wheat loaves were often gritty from sand in the stone-ground flour.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Fisherman: The Nile provided plentiful fish, and tomb paintings show fishermen with nets and boats made of papyrus.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Weaver: Egyptian linen was among the finest in the ancient world, woven from flax, and some mummy wrappings are astonishingly thin.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Jeweler: Jewelers used gold, lapis lazuli and turquoise, and Tutankhamun's tomb held some of the most dazzling pieces ever found.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Programmer: Computers did not exist, though the ancient Egyptians did have careful systems of math and record-keeping.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Astronaut: Egyptians looked up at the stars to build calendars and align pyramids, but space travel was still unthinkable.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Electrician: Egypt had no electricity, but legend says the Dendera carvings show lamps, a claim that scholars reject.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Pilot: There were boat pilots on the Nile, but no pilots of planes, so this job can only be a trap.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Barista: Coffee came to Egypt only centuries later, since it was first brewed in the Arab world in the 1400s.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Photographer: Photography was invented around 1826, over 3,000 years after the pharaohs, so it was a job of painters who made portraits instead.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Radio host: Radio arrived in the 20th century, and Egypt's pharaohs relied on messengers and heralds to spread news.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Train driver: There were no trains, and travel was by boat on the Nile, which flows north, so sails carried boats south.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Influencer: No social media in the Pharaoh's day, though pharaohs did very well at spreading their image on monuments.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Car mechanic: Wheeled chariots arrived with the Hyksos around 1600 BC, but cars were around 3,500 years away.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Typist: Typewriters came in the 1800s, and a scribe's papyrus, brush and ink were the Egyptian equivalent.
Jobs in ancient Egypt.Stockbroker: Markets traded by barter, and stock exchanges would not appear for thousands of years, so no stockbroker could work.

Things that need a license in the US.Driving a car: Each US state issues its own driver's license, but all of them are broadly recognized across state lines.
Things that need a license in the US.Fishing: Most states require a fishing license for adults, and the fees pay for fish stocking and conservation work.
Things that need a license in the US.Hunting: Hunters usually need a license and a tag for each game animal, and many states require a hunter-safety course first.
Things that need a license in the US.Practicing law: Lawyers must pass a state bar exam; in a few states, such as California, you can qualify by studying in a law office rather than attending law school.
Things that need a license in the US.Practicing medicine: Doctors must be licensed by each state's medical board after passing the USMLE exams, so crossing state lines can mean applying again.
Things that need a license in the US.Selling alcohol: Even shops and bars need a license, and some states still restrict liquor sales to state-run stores or ban Sunday sales.
Things that need a license in the US.Flying a plane: A private pilot's certificate from the FAA requires at least 40 hours of flight time, though most students need more.
Things that need a license in the US.Cutting hair: Barbers and cosmetologists need state licenses, often after more than 1,000 hours of training, and rules differ widely between states.
Things that need a license in the US.Selling real estate: Agents need a state license, and in most states they must pass an exam and work under a licensed broker.
Things that need a license in the US.Getting married: Couples need a marriage license, which is the one on this list that's a legal permit rather than a professional qualification.
Things that need a license in the US.Jogging: Public roads and trails are free to run on, with no license required, apart from a few race permits.
Things that need a license in the US.Reading: No one needs permission to read; historically, though, some enslaved people were banned by law from learning to.
Things that need a license in the US.Swimming: Swimming requires no license, but lifeguards and instructors often do need certification.
Things that need a license in the US.Singing: Anyone can sing, though performing copyrighted songs in public usually requires a venue to hold a license from ASCAP or BMI.
Things that need a license in the US.Knitting: No license is needed to knit, and that includes selling your own scarves at a craft fair in many places.
Things that need a license in the US.Riding a bike: Unlike motorcycles, ordinary bicycles need no license in the US, though some cities once required registration.
Things that need a license in the US.Baking at home: Cottage food laws in many states let you sell home-baked goods, usually with limits, though baking for yourself needs nothing.
Things that need a license in the US.Gardening: Home gardening is license-free, although a few towns restrict front-yard vegetable beds.
Things that need a license in the US.Walking a dog: Dogs often need a license in many towns, but the owner doesn't need one to walk them.
Things that need a license in the US.Playing chess: No permit needed; tournaments are organized by clubs and federations, and only the titles like Grandmaster are formally awarded.
Things that need a license in the US.Painting: Painting for fun needs nothing, though a contractor who paints houses for a living may need a state license.
Things that need a license in the US.Whistling: Whistling is free everywhere, and some cultures, such as in the Canary Islands, developed whistled languages.
Things that need a license in the US.Dancing: Dancing needs no license, although a few places once banned it, and a club may require a cabaret license to allow it.
Things that need a license in the US.Juggling: Juggling needs no license; the oldest known depiction of it is in an Egyptian tomb painting about 4,000 years old.

Fictional pigs.Wilbur: E. B. White's runty pig is saved from the butcher by a spider's web messages, in a book that has sold millions of copies.
Fictional pigs.Piglet: The smallest of Pooh's friends was inspired by Christopher Robin Milne's toy, and he is easily frightened but bravely rescues Pooh.
Fictional pigs.Babe: The gallant piglet from the 1995 film, based on Dick King-Smith's The Sheep-Pig, learns to herd sheep by being polite.
Fictional pigs.Napoleon: The tyrannical boar of Orwell's Animal Farm rises to rule by force and is based on Stalin.
Fictional pigs.Snowball: The idealistic pig is chased off Animal Farm by Napoleon's dogs, in a scene echoing Trotsky's fate.
Fictional pigs.Squealer: Napoleon's smooth-talking propagandist in Animal Farm rewrites the farm's commandments, an early example of political spin.
Fictional pigs.Old Major: The prize boar's speech inspires the revolution in Animal Farm, and he dies before it, in a role like Marx or Lenin.
Fictional pigs.Peppa: The British cartoon pig, whose show began in 2004, loves jumping in muddy puddles and lives with her family.
Fictional pigs.Miss Piggy: The Muppets' diva, a karate-chopping star, was created by Jim Henson's team and performed by Frank Oz.
Fictional pigs.Porky: The Looney Tunes stutterer ends the cartoons with "That's all, folks!", a line that is also associated with Bugs Bunny.
Fictional pigs.Olivia: The stylish, high-energy pig of Ian Falconer's picture books was first published in 2000, and was a bestseller.
Fictional pigs.Mr. Toad: The amphibian squire of Toad Hall is a toad, not a pig.
Fictional pigs.Mole: Grahame's burrowing hero is a mammal, but not a pig.
Fictional pigs.Eeyore: The gloomy donkey is Pooh's other friend, not a pig.
Fictional pigs.Templeton: The rat in Charlotte's Web is greedy, but he's the pigs' reluctant ally, not a pig.
Fictional pigs.Babar: Jean de Brunhoff's elephant is a king, not a pig.
Fictional pigs.Snoopy: Charles Schulz's beagle is a dog who sleeps on top of his doghouse.
Fictional pigs.Garfield: Jim Davis's lasagna-loving, lazy cat is far from a pig, though some say he eats like one.
Fictional pigs.Tigger: Pooh's bouncy tiger is a cat, not a pig.
Fictional pigs.Boxer: The loyal cart-horse in Animal Farm works until he collapses, but he is a horse, not a pig.
Fictional pigs.Benjamin: The cynical donkey in Animal Farm sees everything but speaks little; he's not a pig.
Fictional pigs.Mollie: The vain mare of Animal Farm, who loves ribbons and sugar, flees the farm to a better-paid job; not a pig.
Fictional pigs.Charlotte: The wise spider is Wilbur's saviour, not a pig herself.
Fictional pigs.Moses: Animal Farm's raven tells of Sugarcandy Mountain, an obvious jab at organised religion; he is a bird, not a pig.

Materials that come from trees.Paper: Most paper is made from wood pulp, and a single tree can yield only a few thousand sheets of it.
Materials that come from trees.Cardboard: Corrugated cardboard is wood pulp with a fluted middle layer, and it is among the most recycled materials in the world.
Materials that come from trees.Cork: Cork is the bark of the cork oak, which can be harvested every nine years or so without killing the tree.
Materials that come from trees.Plywood: Plywood is made by gluing thin wood veneers with their grains crossed, which makes it more stable than a solid board.
Materials that come from trees.Charcoal: Charcoal is wood heated with little oxygen until only carbon remains, and it has been used in drawing and fuel for thousands of years.
Materials that come from trees.Sawdust: Sawdust is a woodworking byproduct that gets pressed into particleboard and pellets, and is used to smoke foods.
Materials that come from trees.Balsa wood: Balsa is a hardwood botanically, yet it is among the lightest woods around, which is why it's used in model aircraft.
Materials that come from trees.Mahogany: Mahogany was so heavily logged in the Americas that the main species are now protected under international trade rules.
Materials that come from trees.Particleboard: It is made from wood chips and resin pressed into sheets, which makes it a cheap use of sawmill leftovers.
Materials that come from trees.Toilet paper: Americans use about a dozen rolls a month per household, and it is mostly made from trees, either fresh or recycled.
Materials that come from trees.Natural rubber: It is made from latex tapped from the rubber tree, which is native to the Amazon, and tapping does not kill the tree.
Materials that come from trees.Bamboo: A trap: bamboo looks like wood but is a giant grass, and some species grow nearly a metre in a single day.
Materials that come from trees.Cotton: Cotton fibres grow in the seed pod of a shrub, not on a tree.
Materials that come from trees.Wool: Wool is sheep's hair, so it comes from an animal and not from any plant.
Materials that come from trees.Silk: Silk is spun by silkworms, and a single cocoon is one continuous thread up to about a kilometre long.
Materials that come from trees.Leather: Leather is tanned animal hide, though some tanning once used tree bark, which is where "tannin" comes from.
Materials that come from trees.Glass: Glass is mainly melted sand, soda and lime, so no trees are involved.
Materials that come from trees.Steel: It is iron alloyed with a little carbon, mined from ore, though charcoal from wood once fuelled the furnaces.
Materials that come from trees.Nylon: Nylon, made by DuPont in the 1930s, was the first fully synthetic fibre and is derived from petroleum.
Materials that come from trees.Plastic: Most plastic comes from oil and gas, though some early types, such as celluloid, were made from plant cellulose.
Materials that come from trees.Linen: Linen is spun from the flax plant, a herb with fibre in its stem, and it is one of the oldest known textiles.
Materials that come from trees.Clay: Clay is a fine-grained earth made from weathered rock, and nothing in it comes from a tree.
Materials that come from trees.Concrete: Concrete is cement, sand and gravel, and it is the most used man-made material in the world.
Materials that come from trees.Marble: Marble is limestone changed by heat and pressure, so it is stone and no tree has anything to do with it.

Things made of fired clay.Brick: Fired clay bricks have been made for over 5,000 years, and baked ones far outlast sun-dried mud brick.
Things made of fired clay.Terracotta pot: Terracotta means 'baked earth' in Italian, and its porous walls let roots breathe and water evaporate.
Things made of fired clay.Toilet: Most toilets are vitreous china, clay fired at very high temperature and glazed to make it waterproof.
Things made of fired clay.Terracotta Army: Over 8,000 life-size clay soldiers guard China's first emperor, and each one has distinct facial features.
Things made of fired clay.Porcelain teacup: Porcelain is fired at around 1,200 to 1,400 degrees Celsius, which makes it hard and translucent; 'china' comes from its origin.
Things made of fired clay.Roof tile: Clay roof tiles can last over a century, and the Chinese and Mediterranean peoples used them thousands of years ago.
Things made of fired clay.Ocarina: The ocarina is a clay flute whose name means 'little goose' in Italian; some ancient versions are thousands of years old.
Things made of fired clay.Pizza stone: A pizza stone is baked clay that absorbs moisture and stores heat, so crusts crisp as in a brick oven.
Things made of fired clay.Bathroom tile: Ceramic tile is fired clay with a glaze that seals it against water, one of the oldest building materials.
Things made of fired clay.Amphora: Amphorae were clay jars for wine and olive oil; Rome's Monte Testaccio is a hill made of tens of millions of broken ones.
Things made of fired clay.Earthenware jug: Earthenware is clay fired at a lower temperature, so it stays porous unless glazed, and unglazed jugs keep water cool.
Things made of fired clay.Cast iron pan: Cast iron is molten metal poured into molds, not fired clay, and a well-seasoned pan can last generations.
Things made of fired clay.Glass bottle: Glass is melted sand, not clay, and it was being made in Mesopotamia by around 3500 BCE.
Things made of fired clay.Plastic cup: Plastic comes from petroleum-based polymers, not baked clay, and it can persist for centuries.
Things made of fired clay.Wooden bowl: Wood is carved or turned on a lathe, never fired, since a kiln would just turn it to charcoal.
Things made of fired clay.Concrete block: Concrete hardens by a chemical reaction of cement with water rather than by firing, and it keeps curing for years.
Things made of fired clay.Marble statue: Marble is limestone transformed by heat and pressure in the earth, so it is natural stone, not baked clay.
Things made of fired clay.Steel sink: Stainless steel contains at least 10.5 percent chromium, which stops it rusting.
Things made of fired clay.Granite counter: Granite is an igneous rock that crystallized from magma deep underground, with no kiln involved.
Things made of fired clay.Paper plate: Paper plates are pressed wood pulp, usually with a thin coating to stop leaks.
Things made of fired clay.Tin can: The tin can is actually steel coated with tin, and it was invented decades before the can opener.
Things made of fired clay.Wicker basket: Wicker is a weaving technique, not a material, and it is usually made of willow, rattan or reed.
Things made of fired clay.Leather bag: Leather is animal hide treated by tanning so it doesn't rot, a craft thousands of years old.
Things made of fired clay.Styrofoam cup: Foam cups are polystyrene plastic; 'Styrofoam' is actually Dow's trademark for building insulation.

Things with scales.Salmon: Salmon scales grow growth rings like trees, and scientists use them to read a fish's age and its time at sea.
Things with scales.Snake: Snake scales are really folds of the outer skin, and the entire layer is shed in one piece when a snake molts.
Things with scales.Lizard: Many lizards can drop their tails to escape predators, and the scaly tail regrows, though less perfectly.
Things with scales.Pangolin: The pangolin is the only mammal covered in true scales, which are made of keratin, like your fingernails.
Things with scales.Crocodile: Crocodile skin has scales with sensory pits that detect tiny pressure changes in water.
Things with scales.Butterfly wings: Lepidoptera means scale wings: butterfly wings are covered in tiny overlapping scales that produce their colors and patterns.
Things with scales.Dragon: Dragons in myth are scaly, and Chinese dragons are shown with 81 scales, a lucky number made of 9 times 9.
Things with scales.Chicken feet: Chicken legs have scales just like their reptile cousins, a reminder that birds evolved from dinosaurs.
Things with scales.Mermaid tail: Mermaid tails are depicted with fish scales, and in mythology they often shimmer in the sunlight.
Things with scales.Pinecone: Pinecone scales open when dry to release seeds and close when wet, and they work without any living cells.
Things with scales.Iguana: Green iguanas have a sensory third eye on the top of the head that detects light and shadows from above.
Things with scales.Frog: Frogs have smooth moist skin without scales, and they absorb water and even breathe through it.
Things with scales.Dolphin: Dolphins are mammals with smooth rubbery skin, and they shed their outer skin layer every couple of hours.
Things with scales.Blue whale: The blue whale has smooth skin without scales, and it's the largest animal known to have ever lived.
Things with scales.Octopus: Octopuses have soft skin with color-changing cells and no scales, and they have three hearts.
Things with scales.Jellyfish: Jellyfish have no scales or even a brain, and their bodies are about 95 percent water.
Things with scales.Salamander: Salamanders have smooth moist skin without scales, and some can regrow lost limbs and even parts of the heart.
Things with scales.Seal: Seals are covered in fur rather than scales, with a thick blubber layer for insulation.
Things with scales.Penguin: Penguins are covered in tightly packed feathers, which look like fur but never scales.
Things with scales.Hippo: Hippos secrete a reddish oily fluid, nicknamed blood sweat, that acts like sunscreen, and they have no scales.
Things with scales.Toad: Toads have dry, bumpy skin that looks scaly but is warts, and the glands behind their eyes make toxins.
Things with scales.Earthworm: Earthworms have soft, bristly bodies without scales, and they breathe through their skin.
Things with scales.Squid: Squids have soft bodies without scales, and the giant squid has the largest eyes in the animal kingdom.
Things with scales.Elephant: Elephants have thick, wrinkled skin without scales, and the wrinkles help trap moisture to cool them.

Animals famous for being very loud.Howler monkey: Howler monkeys can be heard from about five kilometers away through dense forest, thanks to an enlarged hyoid bone that acts as a resonating chamber.
Animals famous for being very loud.Blue whale: A blue whale's call can top 180 decibels, louder than a jet engine, and may carry for hundreds of kilometers underwater.
Animals famous for being very loud.Lion: A lion's roar can be heard from up to eight kilometers away, and it helps males mark territory across the savanna.
Animals famous for being very loud.Rooster: Roosters crow at around 90 to 100 decibels, and they have a built-in ear protection that keeps them from deafening themselves.
Animals famous for being very loud.Donkey: A donkey's bray, a distinctive hee-haw, can carry for several kilometers across open desert, which suits its wide-ranging habitat.
Animals famous for being very loud.Cicada: Male cicadas produce about 100 decibels with specialized organs called tymbals, and a chorus can rival a lawnmower.
Animals famous for being very loud.Pistol shrimp: The pistol shrimp snaps a claw so fast it creates a cavitation bubble reaching about 200 decibels, which stuns prey and briefly gets hot as the sun's surface.
Animals famous for being very loud.Coqui frog: The tiny coqui, native to Puerto Rico, can call at nearly 100 decibels, and it's so loud in Hawaii that it counts as a pest.
Animals famous for being very loud.Elephant: Elephants trumpet loudly, but they also rumble in infrasound too low for humans to hear, which can travel for kilometers.
Animals famous for being very loud.Peacock: A peacock's piercing call carries far across fields, and males also produce infrasound rumbles during their displays.
Animals famous for being very loud.Sea lion: Sea lions bark loudly and constantly on beaches, and unlike true seals they can rotate their rear flippers to walk on land.
Animals famous for being very loud.Giraffe: Giraffes are mostly silent, though they hum at night, a low sound only discovered in recent decades.
Animals famous for being very loud.Rabbit: Rabbits are quiet animals but can scream loudly when in terror, and they communicate mainly by thumping their hind feet.
Animals famous for being very loud.Snail: Snails are silent, but they have thousands of tiny teeth on a ribbon-like tongue called a radula, which they use to scrape food.
Animals famous for being very loud.Jellyfish: Jellyfish have no brain, heart, or bones, and they drift silently; some species have survived for hundreds of millions of years.
Animals famous for being very loud.Butterfly: Butterflies taste with their feet and are quiet fliers, but some tropical species make clicking sounds with their wings.
Animals famous for being very loud.Starfish: Starfish, properly called sea stars, have no blood, but circulate seawater through their bodies, and they can regrow lost arms.
Animals famous for being very loud.Sea turtle: Sea turtles are mostly silent, though baby turtles can chat with each other inside their eggs before they hatch.
Animals famous for being very loud.Goldfish: Goldfish are quiet, but they can hear well and can distinguish between types of music, as well as live for over 20 years.
Animals famous for being very loud.Ant: Ants are silent to us, but some species communicate by stridulation, rubbing body parts to make tiny squeaks, along with scent trails.
Animals famous for being very loud.Earthworm: Earthworms have no ears and no lungs, breathing through their skin, and they sense vibrations rather than sound.
Animals famous for being very loud.Sloth: Sloths are famously quiet and slow, and they only climb down about once a week to relieve themselves.
Animals famous for being very loud.Ladybug: Ladybugs are silent, and their spots and bright color warn predators that they taste bad.
Animals famous for being very loud.Caterpillar: Caterpillars are silent eaters, though some species make clicking sounds or release scents to warn off predators.

Animals you could see in a real zoo.Giraffe: A giraffe has the same number of neck bones as you, seven, each one up to about 25 cm long, and its heart weighs around 10 kg.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Lion: Lions are the only truly social big cats, living in prides where lionesses do most of the hunting.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Penguin: Penguins' feathers are packed so densely that they form a waterproof coat, and many species see underwater better than in air.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Elephant: An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscle bundles, and it can hold a pea or lift a tree trunk.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Zebra: Each zebra's stripe pattern is unique, and the stripes may deter biting flies, which seem confused by them.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Gorilla: Gorillas are largely vegetarian and beat their chests mostly as a display, and silverback males can weigh around 180 kg.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Hippo: Hippos secrete a reddish oily fluid sometimes called blood sweat that acts as sunscreen and antiseptic, and they can't truly swim.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Meerkat: Meerkats take turns standing guard on hind legs and give different calls to warn of eagles versus snakes.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Flamingo: Flamingos get pink from carotenoid pigments in algae and shrimp, and they can sleep standing on one leg.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Komodo dragon: The world's largest lizard grows up to about 3 metres, and its bite carries venom that lowers blood pressure.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Red panda: This tree dweller isn't closely related to giant pandas, and it uses a fluffy tail as a blanket against the cold.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Tortoise: Some tortoises live over 150 years, and the Aldabra giant tortoise is one of the longest-lived animals known.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Okapi: The okapi looks like a zebra-striped horse but is the giraffe's only living relative, and it wasn't known to science until 1901.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Dodo: The dodo was a flightless bird from Mauritius, driven extinct by the late 1600s after sailors arrived with pigs and rats.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Woolly mammoth: These shaggy relatives of elephants survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago, while pyramids were already built.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Unicorn: The unicorn is a myth, though the horn of a real narwhal was once sold as a unicorn's horn.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Velociraptor: A film star and extinct, the real Velociraptor was about the size of a turkey and covered in feathers.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Griffin: A legendary beast with an eagle's head and a lion's body, and it appears in ancient Persian and Greek art, not in zoos.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Yeti: A legend of the Himalayas, and a 2017 DNA study of purported yeti remains found they were bears.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Sabertooth tiger: Smilodon wasn't really a tiger, and it died out about 10,000 years ago, with fangs up to around 28 cm long.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Pegasus: The winged horse of Greek myth sprang from the blood of Medusa, and it also names a northern constellation.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Quagga: A zebra subspecies striped only at the front, hunted to extinction, and the last known one died in Amsterdam in 1883.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Thylacine: The Tasmanian tiger was a striped marsupial, and the last known one died in a Hobart zoo in 1936.
Animals you could see in a real zoo.Great auk: A flightless seabird of the North Atlantic that was hunted to extinction by 1844, and the original 'penguin'.

Things at a typical birthday party.Candles: Blowing out candles may trace to ancient Greeks, who offered moon-shaped cakes with candles to Artemis. Smoke was thought to carry wishes skyward.
Things at a typical birthday party.Balloons: Latex balloons were first mass-produced in the 1930s. Helium makes them float because it is lighter than air.
Things at a typical birthday party.Birthday cake: Birthday cakes as we know them came from 18th-century Germany, where children's birthdays, 'Kinderfeste', featured a cake with candles.
Things at a typical birthday party.Party hat: The cone party hat is a children's party staple, usually held on by a thin elastic chin strap that stings if it snaps.
Things at a typical birthday party.Presents: Gift giving on birthdays goes back to ancient times, when gifts were thought to ward off evil spirits around a person's special day.
Things at a typical birthday party.Streamers: Crepe paper streamers were invented in the early 1900s. Twisting them over a doorway or ceiling quickly turns any room festive.
Things at a typical birthday party.Piñata: Piñatas likely reached Mexico from Spain, though similar Chinese pots predate them. Early Mexican ones were smashed at church celebrations.
Things at a typical birthday party.Party blower: The party blower, or noisemaker, unrolls with a squeak when you blow. It is often called a 'horn' at birthday celebrations.
Things at a typical birthday party.Goody bag: Goody bags are small thank-you gifts handed to guests on leaving. Party favors like these are meant to send everyone home happy.
Things at a typical birthday party.Birthday card: Printed birthday cards took off in Victorian England, when cheap postage made posting greetings popular.
Things at a typical birthday party.Ice cream: Ice cream is often served alongside the cake. It was a luxury for centuries before freezers made it cheap.
Things at a typical birthday party.Wedding veil: A veil belongs at weddings, not birthday parties. Roman brides wore a flame-colored veil to ward off evil spirits.
Things at a typical birthday party.Coffin: A coffin belongs at a funeral. Even if the guest of honor is getting older, birthday parties don't call for one.
Things at a typical birthday party.Gavel: A gavel is a small mallet used by judges and auctioneers, so it belongs in a courtroom or auction hall, not at a party.
Things at a typical birthday party.Mortarboard: This flat-topped cap is worn at graduations. Its square shape reportedly resembles the board bricklayers hold mortar on.
Things at a typical birthday party.Menorah: A menorah is lit during Hanukkah, with eight branches plus a helper candle. It is a festival lamp, never a birthday decoration.
Things at a typical birthday party.Hearse: A hearse carries a coffin to a funeral, so a party with one would be a very unusual birthday surprise.
Things at a typical birthday party.Diploma: A diploma is handed over at graduation. The word comes from the Greek for a paper folded double.
Things at a typical birthday party.Ballot box: A ballot box holds votes at elections, so it belongs at polling stations and not at a cake-and-balloons party.
Things at a typical birthday party.Tombstone: A tombstone marks a grave. It is the opposite of birthday cheer, a monument to the end of a life.
Things at a typical birthday party.Bridal bouquet: A bouquet is carried by a bride at her wedding. Tossing it is a tradition said to predict the next bride.
Things at a typical birthday party.Jury box: The jury box seats jurors during a courtroom trial. It is a place of serious judgment, a far cry from cake and balloons.
Things at a typical birthday party.Advent wreath: The Advent wreath holds candles lit through the weeks before Christmas, which belongs to a church season, not a birthday.
Things at a typical birthday party.Pallbearer: Pallbearers carry a coffin at a funeral. That makes them the very opposite of the cheerful guests at a birthday party.

Types of coat or jacket.Parka: The parka was developed by the Inuit, who made it from caribou or seal skin. The word comes from the Nenets language of Siberia.
Types of coat or jacket.Trench coat: The trench coat was developed for British officers in World War I. Burberry and Aquascutum both claim to have invented it.
Types of coat or jacket.Blazer: The blazer may be named after HMS Blazer, whose captain dressed the crew in smart jackets for a royal visit in the 1800s.
Types of coat or jacket.Anorak: The anorak is a hooded waterproof jacket from the Greenlandic Inuit word 'annoraaq'. In Britain it's also slang for an obsessive hobbyist.
Types of coat or jacket.Peacoat: The peacoat is a short, heavy wool coat first worn by sailors. Its double-breasted front and wide lapels kept out sea winds.
Types of coat or jacket.Duffel coat: The duffel coat is a hooded wool coat with toggles, named for a Belgian town, Duffel. Paddington Bear wears one.
Types of coat or jacket.Bomber jacket: The bomber jacket began as warm flight gear for pilots in World War I, with cuffs and a waistband to block the draft.
Types of coat or jacket.Windbreaker: A windbreaker is a thin, light jacket that blocks wind. Its name is a literal description.
Types of coat or jacket.Overcoat: An overcoat is a long coat worn over other clothes in cold weather. Wool ones were a Victorian gentleman's standard.
Types of coat or jacket.Raincoat: Charles Macintosh patented waterproof fabric in 1824, and in Britain a raincoat is still sometimes called a mac.
Types of coat or jacket.Puffer jacket: Puffer jackets were invented by Eddie Bauer in 1936, after he nearly died of hypothermia, and are quilted with down.
Types of coat or jacket.Denim jacket: The denim jacket came from Levi Strauss in the 1900s as a worker's garment. It later became a mark of rebellion.
Types of coat or jacket.Tailcoat: A tailcoat has a front cut short at the waist and long tails behind. It is worn for white-tie occasions and by orchestra conductors.
Types of coat or jacket.Blouse: A blouse is a loose shirt for the upper body. It is an everyday top worn by itself, not a coat or jacket for outdoor weather.
Types of coat or jacket.Tunic: A tunic is a long, simple shirt-like garment from ancient Rome. It's worn alone and not as an outer layer.
Types of coat or jacket.Kilt: A kilt is a Scottish wrap skirt, which is worn on the lower body. It isn't a coat or jacket.
Types of coat or jacket.Sarong: A sarong is a wrap-around cloth skirt worn around the waist in Southeast Asia and the Pacific, not a jacket.
Types of coat or jacket.Leggings: Leggings cover the legs and aren't outerwear for the torso, so they are not a coat or jacket in any sense.
Types of coat or jacket.Tank top: The tank top is named after swimming tanks, or 'tank suits', worn at pools in the 1920s. It's a sleeveless shirt.
Types of coat or jacket.Polo shirt: The polo shirt was designed by tennis star René Lacoste in the 1920s. The collar and breathable cotton made it good for sport.
Types of coat or jacket.Camisole: A camisole is a light, sleeveless undergarment or top with thin straps, so it is not an outer layer like a coat or jacket.
Types of coat or jacket.Romper: A romper is a one-piece outfit with short legs. It began as clothing for toddlers and is not a coat or jacket.
Types of coat or jacket.Toga: The toga was a draped garment of ancient Rome, worn only by citizens, so it was not a jacket.
Types of coat or jacket.Sari: A sari is a long unstitched cloth draped around the body in South Asia, so it isn't a coat.

Legendary places that never existed.Atlantis: Plato described this island empire around 360 BC, swallowed by the sea in a single day. It was probably a parable, not a real place.
Legendary places that never existed.El Dorado: The "golden one" was first a king dusted in gold, then a legendary city. The myth sent explorers into South America for centuries.
Legendary places that never existed.Shangri-La: Imagined by James Hilton in the 1933 novel Lost Horizon: a hidden Himalayan paradise where people barely age.
Legendary places that never existed.Avalon: The mythical isle where King Arthur's Excalibur was forged, and where he was taken to heal. Its name is linked to "apple."
Legendary places that never existed.Camelot: Arthur's court was not in the earliest legends. Chretien de Troyes first named it in the 12th century.
Legendary places that never existed.Valhalla: In Norse myth, Odin's hall where warriors slain in battle feast and fight every day until Ragnarok.
Legendary places that never existed.Asgard: The Norse gods' realm, linked to the human world by the rainbow bridge Bifrost. Marvel made it famous.
Legendary places that never existed.Lemuria: A sunken continent invented in the 1800s to explain similar lemur fossils in Madagascar and India. Plate tectonics later explained it.
Legendary places that never existed.Hyperborea: A Greek land beyond the North Wind, where sunlit people lived in bliss and Apollo spent his winters.
Legendary places that never existed.Lyonesse: An Arthurian land said to lie between Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, drowned beneath the sea.
Legendary places that never existed.Tir na nOg: Irish for "Land of the Youth." The hero Oisin spent what felt like three years there, but 300 passed at home.
Legendary places that never existed.Cockaigne: The medieval land of plenty, where roasted geese fly into mouths and the rivers run with wine.
Legendary places that never existed.Timbuktu: Real, and in Mali. Once a major hub of Islamic learning, it's often used as a byword for the ends of the earth.
Legendary places that never existed.Machu Picchu: A real Inca citadel in Peru, built about 1450. Hiram Bingham brought it world fame in 1911.
Legendary places that never existed.Petra: A real city in Jordan carved into rose-red cliffs by the Nabataeans, who grew rich on the spice trade.
Legendary places that never existed.Troy: Once thought pure legend, until Heinrich Schliemann dug at Hisarlik in Turkey. The city was real, though the horse is a story.
Legendary places that never existed.Babylon: Real ruins in Iraq, once a great Mesopotamian city. Only the Hanging Gardens may be a myth.
Legendary places that never existed.Angkor Wat: Real: Cambodia's vast temple complex from the early 1100s, and the largest religious monument in the world.
Legendary places that never existed.Samarkand: A real Silk Road city in Uzbekistan, inhabited for over 2,500 years. Its name just sounds like a fairy-tale place.
Legendary places that never existed.Pompeii: Real: the Roman town buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, which preserved streets, bakeries and graffiti.
Legendary places that never existed.Zanzibar: Real, an island spice hub off Tanzania, and birthplace of Freddie Mercury. Its name sounds fairy-tale.
Legendary places that never existed.Kathmandu: The real capital of Nepal, in a valley dotted with UNESCO temples. The name sounds mythic but it's a busy modern city.

Hebrew letters (not Greek).Alef: The first letter is silent at the start of a word, and it was originally from a picture of an ox head, as was the Greek alpha.

Hebrew letters (not Greek).Gimel: The third letter, whose name probably means camel, has numerical value three in Hebrew numerals.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Dalet: The fourth letter means door, and it is the ancestor of the Greek delta and the Latin D.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Hey: The fifth letter, also spelled He, is an airy H sound and has the numerical value five.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Vav: The sixth letter means hook, and it is also used as a connecting word meaning 'and' at the start of words.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Zayin: The seventh letter's name means weapon in Hebrew, and has the numeric value seven.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Chet: The eighth letter is a throaty sound similar to the ch in loch, and it is also the first letter of the word chai, life.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Yod: The tenth letter is the smallest of the alphabet, and a Hebrew phrase about a 'jot' comes from its Greek name iota.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Lamed: It is the tallest Hebrew letter, and it has a value of 30, and it is a part of the word Torah study.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Nun: The 14th letter means fish, and it has a final form used when it ends a word.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Shin: This is a letter with three prongs often printed on a mezuzah, standing for one of the names of God, Shaddai.

Hebrew letters (not Greek).Gamma: The third Greek letter, named in gamma rays, and not Hebrew, whose third letter is gimel.

Hebrew letters (not Greek).Theta: A Greek letter with no Hebrew counterpart by name, used in maths for angles.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Lambda: A Greek letter used as the symbol of Half-Life and of the Spartans' shields, and Hebrew has lamed.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Sigma: This Greek letter is used for summation in maths, and it is not Hebrew.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Omega: The last Greek letter, meaning big O, which gave the phrase 'alpha and omega'. Hebrew's last is tav.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Kappa: A Greek letter, whose Hebrew cousin is kaf, and kappa itself is Greek.
Hebrew letters (not Greek).Omicron: The Greek letter meaning little o, so named to tell it apart from omega, and it is Greek.

Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Pheasant: Native to Asia, it was brought to Europe long ago. Males flaunt iridescent plumage and long tails.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Quail: These small, plump birds lay speckled eggs, and the Japanese quail has even flown aboard space missions.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Partridge: The partridge in a pear tree of the Christmas carol is probably the grey or red-legged partridge.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Grouse: Males perform strutting displays in groups called leks, and the red grouse is a Scottish moorland bird.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Peacock: Strictly the male peafowl, a member of the pheasant family, whose tail feathers can reach over a metre and a half.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Guinea fowl: Native to Africa, they are noisy watchdogs of the farmyard and are a type of Galliforme.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Ptarmigan: A grouse that turns white in winter for camouflage in snow, and it also feathers its feet like snowshoes.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Bantam: Not a species but a small chicken breed, and the name comes from the Indonesian port of Bantam.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Junglefowl: The wild ancestors of the domestic chicken live in the forests of Southeast Asia.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Capercaillie: The biggest grouse, it is a turkey-sized forest bird of Eurasia, and males are quite aggressive in the breeding season.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Duck: It belongs to the Anseriformes, the waterfowl, a different order from chickens.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Goose: A waterfowl in Anseriformes, so it is not a chicken relative, but it is known for its V-shaped flights.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Swan: Another waterfowl, in the same order as ducks and geese, which is not the same as Galliformes.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Pigeon: Belongs to the order Columbiformes, with doves, and not to the chicken family.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Ostrich: A flightless bird in its own group, the ratites, and the largest bird alive. It is not close to chickens.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Emu: A flightless Australian ratite, which is the second tallest bird, and is not a Galliforme.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Eagle: A bird of prey, in the same group as hawks, which is quite a different order from the chickens.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Owl: Owls make up their own order, Strigiformes, and have no close tie with the chicken family.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Parrot: A parrot belongs to the Psittaciformes, a different order, and is known for mimicry.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Heron: A wading bird of the Pelecaniformes, and it is far from the chickens in the family tree.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Crow: A songbird, in Passeriformes, whose members are known for their brains, unlike Galliformes.
Chicken-family birds (Galliformes).Dove: A relative of the pigeon in Columbiformes, so it is not a chicken relative.
